arXiv:2607.28429v2 [math.MG] 10 Aug 2026
Nearly Sharp Bounds for Lattice Coverings by Convex Bodies
Heng Li
††thanks: School of Mathematics, Shandong University, Jinan, China, and Extremal Combinatorics and Probability Group, Institute for Basic Science, Daejeon, South Korea. Email:˜heng.li@sdu.edu.cn.
Xizhi Liu
††thanks: School of Mathematical Sciences, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, China. Email:˜liuxizhi@ustc.edu.cn.
Abstract
For an n-dimensional convex body K, let \theta_{L}(K) denote its lattice covering density, and let \Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{conv}}(n) and \Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{sym}}(n) be the corresponding worst-case quantities over all convex bodies and over origin-symmetric convex bodies, respectively.
Before this work, these quantities were known only to lie between a lower bound of order n and an upper bound of order n^{2}, so even their polynomial order was undetermined.
We prove that there are absolute constants c,C>0 such that
cn\log n\leq\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{sym}}(n)\leq\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{conv}}(n)\leq Cn\log n\,(\log\log n)^{10/3+o(1)}.
Thus both worst-case quantities are n\log n\,(\log n)^{o(1)}, and the upper and lower bounds differ by a factor at most (\log\log n)^{10/3+o(1)}.
For the upper bound, a vertical–horizontal amplification based on weighted Boolean cubes combines covering estimates for low-codimensional sections into an exact lattice covering of an arbitrary convex body.
For the lower bound, a random-slab construction and Poisson witnesses on flat tori show, with positive probability, that the resulting body admits no lattice covering of density below cn\log n.
Keywords. Lattice covering; convex body; geometry of numbers; finite-field Kakeya; random slabs; Poisson process.
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification. 11H31, 52C17, 52A23, 60D05.
1 Introduction
1.1 Lattice coverings and the extremal problem
A convex body in \mathbb{R}^{n} is a compact convex set with nonempty interior.
If v_{1},\ldots,v_{n} is a basis of a full-rank lattice \Lambda\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}, write \det\Lambda\coloneqq|\det(v_{1},\ldots,v_{n})| for its positive covolume.
The translates \{K+\lambda\colon\lambda\in\Lambda\} form a lattice covering if
\Lambda+K\coloneqq\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Lambda}(\lambda+K)=\mathbb{R}^{n}.
The density of this covering is \operatorname{vol}_{n}(K)/\det\Lambda.
The lattice covering density of K is
\theta_{L}(K)\coloneqq\inf\left\{\frac{\operatorname{vol}_{n}(K)}{\det\Lambda}\colon\Lambda+K=\mathbb{R}^{n}\right\}.
This quantity is invariant under invertible affine transformations of K.
We study the largest possible lattice covering density in a fixed dimension.
Define
\displaystyle\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{conv}}(n)
\displaystyle\coloneqq\sup\left\{\theta_{L}(K)\colon K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\text{ is a convex body}\right\},
\displaystyle\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{sym}}(n)
\displaystyle\coloneqq\sup\left\{\theta_{L}(K)\colon K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\text{ is an origin-symmetric convex body}\right\}.
The defining classes immediately give \Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{sym}}(n)\leq\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{conv}}(n).
All logarithms are natural unless a base is displayed, and all asymptotic statements involving n are taken as n\to\infty.
In the upper-bound construction, statements involving only the auxiliary dimension d are taken as d\to\infty.
For positive quantities a and b, write a\asymp b if a/b is bounded above and below by positive absolute constants in the relevant limit, and write a\gg b if a/b\to\infty.
Rogers [29] gives a classical treatment of packing and covering.
For the broader geometry of numbers, see Gruber and Lekkerkerker [16]; Conway and Sloane [4] give an extensive account of lattices and sphere packings.
1.2 Previous bounds
For comparison, Rogers [26] proved that arbitrary translates cover every n-dimensional convex body with density n\log n+n\log\log n+O(n), while Fejes Tóth [11] obtained essentially the same density using O(\log n) cosets of one lattice.
The restriction to a single lattice is substantially harder.
For Euclidean balls, Dumer [6] obtained the sharper translative bound (1/2+o(1))n\log n, and Bukh, Gao, Liu, Pikhurko, and Sun [2] attained this density with controlled covering multiplicity and identified a limitation of random periodic constructions.
For lattice coverings, Rogers [28] proved the universal estimate \theta_{L}(K)\leq n^{\log_{2}\log n+O(1)}.
Ordentlich, Regev, and Weiss [23] established the first polynomial universal bound, \theta_{L}(K)\leq Cn^{2}.
In subsequent work, the same authors [24] obtained uniform multiplicity estimates at polynomial covering density and studied random Construction-A lattices.
Near-linear upper bounds with polylogarithmic losses were already known for bodies with sufficiently many orthogonal symmetries through Gritzmann [15], and for locally anti-blocking bodies and polytopes with few vertices through Schymura, Wang, and Xue [32].
For Euclidean unit balls B_{2}^{n}, Gao, Liu, Pikhurko, and Sun [13] proved
\theta_{L}(B_{2}^{n})=O\bigl(n(\log n)^{\beta_{\mathrm{ball}}}\bigr),\quad\text{where}\quad\beta_{\mathrm{ball}}\coloneqq\frac{1}{2}\log_{2}\left(\frac{8\pi e}{3\sqrt{3}}\right)=1.85837\ldots.
In the opposite direction, Coxeter, Few, and Rogers [5] proved \theta_{L}(B_{2}^{n})\geq(e^{-3/2}+o(1))n.
Together with the universal estimate of Ordentlich, Regev, and Weiss [23], this gave the following bounds before the present work:
(e^{-3/2}+o(1))n\leq\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{sym}}(n)\leq\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{conv}}(n)\leq Cn^{2}.
These estimates left a multiplicative gap of order n; in particular, even the polynomial order of the worst-case lattice covering density was unknown.
1.3 Main results
The results of this paper narrow this polynomial gap to an iterated-logarithmic factor and place both extremal quantities at the n\log n scale in the following precise sense.
Theorem 1.1.
There exist absolute constants c,C>0 and a nonnegative sequence \varepsilon_{n}\to 0 such that, for all sufficiently large n,
cn\log n\leq\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{sym}}(n)\leq\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{conv}}(n)\leq Cn\log n\,(\log\log n)^{10/3+\varepsilon_{n}}.
Theorem 1.1 follows from the following two independent results.
The first gives a universal upper bound for every convex body.
Theorem 1.2.
There exist an absolute constant C>0 and a nonnegative sequence \varepsilon_{n}\to 0 such that, for all sufficiently large n,
\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{conv}}(n)\leq Cn\log n\,(\log\log n)^{10/3+\varepsilon_{n}}.
Remark.
The exponent 10/3 of \log\log n in Theorem 1.2 can be reduced to \frac{2}{3}\log_{2}(2\pi e)=2.72946\ldots by the two-stage binary correction developed in our companion note [21].
Our main goal in the present paper is to identify the n\log n scale up to an iterated-logarithmic factor, rather than to optimize the exponent of \log\log n.
The second constructs origin-symmetric bodies with large lattice covering density.
Theorem 1.3.
There is an absolute constant c>0 such that, for every sufficiently large integer n, there is an origin-symmetric convex body K_{n}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} such that
\theta_{L}(K_{n})\geq cn\log n.
The witness K_{n} constructed in the proof of Theorem 1.3 is already in John position, with John ellipsoid B_{2}^{n}.
Since (\log\log n)^{10/3+o(1)}=(\log n)^{o(1)}, Theorem 1.1 gives
\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{sym}}(n)=n\log n\,(\log n)^{o(1)}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{conv}}(n)=n\log n\,(\log n)^{o(1)}.
Thus the worst-case lattice covering density is determined up to a factor (\log\log n)^{10/3+o(1)}.
The upper bound also confirms and strengthens the conjecture of Schymura, Wang, and Xue [32, Remark 1.4] that \theta_{L}(K)\leq Cn(\log n)^{1+\log_{2}e} for every n-dimensional convex body K.
For Euclidean balls, the universal upper bound asymptotically improves the factor (\log n)^{\beta_{\mathrm{ball}}} obtained by Gao, Liu, Pikhurko, and Sun [13] to \log n\,(\log\log n)^{10/3+o(1)}.
1.4 Ideas behind the upper bound
Choose an auxiliary dimension d much smaller than n, write n=m+d, and split \mathbb{R}^{n}=E\oplus F with \dim E=m and \dim F=d.
For y\in F, let K_{y}\coloneqq\{x\in E\colon x+y\in K\} be the horizontal section of K at height y.
The vertical space F is used to find a useful family of such sections above every translate, and the horizontal space E is used to cover them.
The challenge is to do this when the sections have different volumes and then encode all vertical and horizontal shifts in a single lattice.
To find useful heights, we fold a narrow Gaussian into the unit cube.
Each base point determines Gaussian weights on its Boolean vertices.
The folding identity separates the total weight of the cube from the way this weight is divided among its vertices.
Entropy estimates show that no single vertex receives too much weight and that vertices with very small weights can later be removed while retaining almost all of the total.
Good base points must be available above every vertical translate.
We select a movable information layer on which the total weight and both entropy bounds are controlled, and divide the unit cube into a finite-field grid.
The high-rank Kakeya theorem of Kopparty, Lev, Saraf, and Sudan [20] gives a linear subspace such that every grid cell can be shifted into this layer.
Construction A lifts the subspace to a lattice in F.
Every vertical translate then contains a Boolean cube with total normalized Gaussian weight d^{-5/2+o(1)} and the required entropy bounds.
We next place K in isotropic position.
The pointwise marginal theorem of Eldan and Klartag [9] supplies a low-dimensional subspace F on which the section volumes satisfy
\operatorname{vol}_{m}(K_{y})=\bigl(1+o(1)\bigr)\operatorname{vol}_{n}(K)\gamma_{d}(y)
throughout the relevant range.
A finite discretization replaces these sections by finitely many slightly smaller convex bodies while retaining their individual volumes.
The mean-hole estimates of Rogers [27] and Schmidt [30] provide one horizontal lattice that works for every retained section.
Shannon entropy controls the total load lost in pruning, while min-entropy keeps every remaining section within the range of the mean-hole estimate.
Finally, simultaneous horizontal shifts multiply the remaining uncovered proportions, and a finite-index shear incorporates all shifts into one lattice in E\oplus F.
A total horizontal load of order n\log n makes the uncovered proportion small enough for Rogers’ completion lemma [28], which turns the almost covering into an exact one.
The vertical construction costs d^{5/2+o(1)}.
The min-entropy requirement leads to
d=(\log\log n)^{4/3+o(1)},
so the vertical loss is (\log\log n)^{10/3+o(1)}.
1.5 Ideas behind the lower bound
The lower-bound construction intersects a Euclidean ball and a cube with a Poisson family of slabs.
In the normalization used later, a=2, b=ae^{1/n}, and
K_{\Pi}=bB_{2}^{n}\cap[-1,1]^{n}\cap\bigcap_{u\in\Pi}\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\colon|\langle u,x\rangle|\leq 1\}.
The expected volume of this body is comparable to \kappa_{n}a^{n}, and a fixed positive proportion of the realizations have volume of this order.
The Euclidean ball gives a uniform outer-radius cutoff, the random slabs create the obstructions to covering, and the cube places the construction directly in John position.
Indeed, the inclusions B_{2}^{n}\subseteq K_{\Pi}\subseteq[-1,1]^{n}, together with the cube’s contact points, show that the John ellipsoid is exactly B_{2}^{n}.
Fix a lattice \Lambda and a target y\in\mathbb{R}^{n}/\Lambda.
Choose a representative \widetilde{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.
Each residual vector \widetilde{y}-\lambda, with \lambda\in\Lambda, determines a spherical cap of slab normals that remove it.
For the targets used in the proof, all relevant residuals lie in a thin shell.
The target is uncovered when every corresponding cap is hit by the Poisson process, so the problem becomes one of constructing and controlling simultaneous Poisson witnesses.
The caps belonging to one target can be strongly dependent.
We cluster nearby caps and place a measurable slot in the common intersection of each cluster.
An injective choice of one Poisson point from every slot witnesses that the target is a hole.
A hierarchical common-lens estimate controls the activity of these witnesses and their self-interactions.
A greedy packing on the flat torus supplies
T=\exp\bigl((1/2-o(1))n\log n\bigr)
targets whose residual directions are separated across different targets.
The packing remains valid in the cusps of lattice space because the image of a Euclidean ball in a flat torus has Haar measure at most its Euclidean volume divided by \det\Lambda.
A continuous Poisson version of Janson’s inequality then makes the covering probability superpolynomially small for each fixed lattice.
Finally, every lattice that could cover the random body has bounded covering radius and therefore a short basis.
A stable net over these basis matrices makes the estimate uniform over all lattices.
The same n\log n scale emerges from different balances in the two proofs.
In the upper-bound argument, exponential decay in the total horizontal load means that a sufficiently large constant multiple of n\log n reaches the (n^{n}+1)^{-1} threshold required by Rogers’ completion lemma.
In the lower-bound argument, the target supply above absorbs the self-interaction cost e^{O(R)} of the Poisson witnesses throughout R\leq cn\log n, where R\coloneqq\kappa_{n}a^{n}/\det\Lambda.
Excluding every lattice in this range forces any covering lattice to have determinant smaller than \kappa_{n}a^{n}/(cn\log n), which yields the lower bound.
The remaining gap between Theorems 1.2 and 1.3 is the iterated-logarithmic factor.
1.6 Organization
The proof has two technically independent parts.
Part I proves the universal upper bound.
In Section 2, we fix the notation and state the external results used in that argument.
In Section 3, we develop the weighted full-cube construction.
In Section 4, we transfer its weights to sections of an arbitrary convex body and perform the finite-index lifting.
In Section 5, we combine these ingredients to prove Theorem 1.2.
Part II proves the worst-case lower bound.
In Section 6, we collect the spherical-cap, flat-torus, and Poisson tools.
In Section 7, we define the random body and prove its volume and normalization properties.
In Section 8, we construct good separated targets for a fixed lattice.
In Section 9, we develop the common-lens Poisson witness method and prove the fixed-lattice estimate.
In Section 10, we pass from one lattice to all lattices.
Finally, in Section 11, we prove Theorem 1.3 and complete the proof of Theorem 1.1.
Part I Universal upper bounds
2 Tools for the upper bound
This section fixes the quotient-torus notation and states the four principal external inputs used in the proof: the Rogers–Schmidt mean-hole estimate [27, 30], Rogers’ completion lemma [28], the pointwise Gaussian marginal theorem of Eldan and Klartag [9], and the high-rank finite-field Kakeya bound of Kopparty, Lev, Saraf, and Sudan [20].
For a positive integer N, write [N]\coloneqq\{1,\ldots,N\}.
For R>0, let B_{R}^{r}\coloneqq\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{r}\colon\lVert x\rVert_{2}\leq R\}.
If \Lambda\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{r} is a full-rank lattice, let \mathbb{T}_{\Lambda}\coloneqq\mathbb{R}^{r}/\Lambda be the quotient torus.
Let \mu_{\Lambda} be the normalized Lebesgue measure on \mathbb{T}_{\Lambda}, equivalently its Haar probability measure.
Thus \mu_{\Lambda} is the unique translation-invariant probability measure on \mathbb{T}_{\Lambda}.
Let \pi_{\Lambda}\colon\mathbb{R}^{r}\to\mathbb{T}_{\Lambda} be the quotient map.
For a Borel set J\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{r}, define the uncovered proportion
\bar{\rho}(\Lambda+J)\coloneqq 1-\mu_{\Lambda}(\pi_{\Lambda}(J)).
A full-rank lattice L\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{r} is unimodular if \det L=1.
Let \mathcal{L}_{r} denote the space of unimodular lattices in \mathbb{R}^{r}, and let \mu_{r} be the normalized \operatorname{SL}_{r}(\mathbb{R})-invariant probability measure on \mathcal{L}_{r}, with the normalization used in Siegel’s mean-value theorem [33].
Set b_{0}\coloneqq\frac{1}{4}\log\frac{27}{16} and \eta_{r}\coloneqq b_{0}r-3\log r.
Let \operatorname{GL}_{r}(\mathbb{R}) denote the group of invertible r\times r real matrices, acting as linear maps on \mathbb{R}^{r}.
If A\in\operatorname{GL}_{r}(\mathbb{R}), then \theta_{L}(A(K))=\theta_{L}(K) and \bar{\rho}(A(\Lambda)+A(J))=\bar{\rho}(\Lambda+J).
Translations of the body leave both quantities unchanged.
We shall therefore use affine normalizations and determinant-one shears without further comment.
The following formulation of the mean-hole estimate is recorded by Ordentlich, Regev, and Weiss [23, Theorem 2.3].
It originates in Rogers’ mean-value argument [27]; see also Schmidt’s closely related estimates [30].
Theorem 2.1.
There exists an absolute constant c_{\mathrm{RS}}>0 such that, for every sufficiently large r and every Borel set J\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{r} of volume V\leq\eta_{r},
\left|\int_{\mathcal{L}_{r}}\bar{\rho}(L+J)\,\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{r}(L)-e^{-V}\right|<c_{\mathrm{RS}}e^{-\eta_{r}}.
The theorem applies to arbitrary Borel sets and hence to all labels for sections of varying volume used later.
More precisely, if the desired lattice determinant is D_{h}, scaling to determinant one replaces a set J by D_{h}^{-1/r}J, whose volume is \operatorname{vol}_{r}(J)/D_{h}.
This normalized volume is the load used in the horizontal argument.
The upper restriction V\leq\eta_{r} is the reason for controlling the largest load at a Boolean vertex by min-entropy.
The last step of the argument uses Rogers’ completion lemma [28, Lemma 4] to turn a lattice with sufficiently small uncovered proportion into an exact covering.
Lemma 2.2.
Let C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{r} be a convex body and let \Lambda\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{r} be a lattice.
If \bar{\rho}(\Lambda+C)\leq(r^{r}+1)^{-1}, then \Lambda+\left(1+\frac{1}{r}\right)C=\mathbb{R}^{r}.
We next record the pointwise Gaussian marginal estimate of Eldan and Klartag [9, Theorem 1].
Its role is to compare, simultaneously at every point of a low-dimensional ball, the volume of a section of an isotropic convex body with the standard Gaussian density.
For y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, write \gamma_{d}(y)\coloneqq(2\pi)^{-d/2}e^{-\lVert y\rVert_{2}^{2}/2}.
We use the pointwise, rather than merely distributional, form of the central limit theorem for low-dimensional marginals of log-concave measures.
Write G_{n,d} for the Grassmannian of d-dimensional linear subspaces of \mathbb{R}^{n}, equipped with its rotation-invariant probability measure.
For a random vector X with log-concave density f_{X}, choose the upper-semicontinuous log-concave representative of f_{X}.
If F\in G_{n,d}, E\coloneqq F^{\perp}, and P_{F} denotes orthogonal projection onto F, define the F-marginal density of X by
\rho_{F}(y)\coloneqq\int_{E}f_{X}(x+y)\,\,\mathrm{d}x,\quad\text{for }y\in F.
This is the marginal operator used by Eldan and Klartag.
By Prékopa’s theorem, \rho_{F} is log-concave and hence continuous on the interior of its support.
Theorem 2.3.
There exist universal constants C,c_{1},c_{2},c_{3},c_{4}>0 with the following property.
Let X be an isotropic random vector in \mathbb{R}^{n} with a log-concave density, and let 1\leq d\leq n^{c_{1}} be an integer.
Then there is a set \mathcal{E}\subseteq G_{n,d} of measure at least 1-Ce^{-n^{c_{2}}} such that, for every F\in\mathcal{E}, the density \rho_{F} defined above satisfies
\left|\frac{\rho_{F}(y)}{\gamma_{d}(y)}-1\right|\leq Cn^{-c_{3}}
(2.1)
whenever y\in F and \lVert y\rVert_{2}\leq n^{c_{4}}.
Suppose that X is uniform on an isotropic convex body K, and fix f_{X}\coloneqq\mathbf{1}_{K}/\operatorname{vol}_{n}(K).
Let E\coloneqq F^{\perp} and m\coloneqq n-d.
For y\in F, define the horizontal section K_{y}\coloneqq\{x\in E\colon x+y\in K\}.
The defining integral now gives
\rho_{F}(y)=\frac{\operatorname{vol}_{m}(K_{y})}{\operatorname{vol}_{n}(K)}
for every y\in F.
On \operatorname{int}(P_{F}(K)), the Brunn–Minkowski inequality [31, Section 7.1] also shows directly that y\mapsto\operatorname{vol}_{m}(K_{y})^{1/m} is continuous.
The topological support of the projected measure is exactly P_{F}(K).
The inclusion of the support in P_{F}(K) follows from compactness.
Conversely, every relative neighborhood of a point of P_{F}(K) meets \operatorname{int}(P_{F}(K)), where the section-volume function is positive, and therefore has positive projected measure.
In particular, \rho_{F} is positive and continuous on \operatorname{int}(P_{F}(K)).
Thus, once F is chosen as in Theorem 2.3, the theorem compares \operatorname{vol}_{m}(K_{y})/\operatorname{vol}_{n}(K) with \gamma_{d}(y) at every y\in F satisfying \lVert y\rVert_{2}\leq n^{c_{4}}.
This pointwise conclusion, rather than merely a distributional approximation, is what the vertical construction requires.
The fourth principal input collected here is a high-rank finite-field Kakeya theorem.
The polynomial method for finite-field Kakeya sets began with Dvir’s rank-one theorem [7].
Dvir, Kopparty, Saraf, and Sudan [8] later developed the multiplicity method and several extensions.
Here we use the rank-k theorem of Kopparty, Lev, Saraf, and Sudan [20, Theorem 1], stated below in the form we need.
Let q be a prime power, let 1\leq k\leq d-1, and let \operatorname{Gr}_{d,k}(\mathbb{F}_{q}) denote the set of k-dimensional linear subspaces of \mathbb{F}_{q}^{d}.
A set A\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{q}^{d} is a Kakeya set of rank k if, for every C\in\operatorname{Gr}_{d,k}(\mathbb{F}_{q}), the set A contains a translate of C.
Theorem 2.4.
If A\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{q}^{d} is a Kakeya set of rank k, then
|A|\geq\left(1+(q-1)q^{-k}\right)^{-d}q^{d}.
The form needed in the vertical construction is the following direct contrapositive.
Corollary 2.5.
Define the rank-k Kakeya threshold by
\vartheta_{d,q,k}\coloneqq 1-\left(1+(q-1)q^{-k}\right)^{-d}.
(2.2)
If B\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{q}^{d} satisfies |B|/q^{d}>\vartheta_{d,q,k}, then there exists C\in\operatorname{Gr}_{d,k}(\mathbb{F}_{q}) such that B+C=\mathbb{F}_{q}^{d}.
Proof.
Suppose instead that B+C\neq\mathbb{F}_{q}^{d} for every C\in\operatorname{Gr}_{d,k}(\mathbb{F}_{q}).
For each such C, some affine coset of C is disjoint from B and hence is contained in A\coloneqq\mathbb{F}_{q}^{d}\setminus B.
Thus A is a Kakeya set of rank k.
By Theorem 2.4, |A|\geq\left(1+(q-1)q^{-k}\right)^{-d}q^{d}, contrary to the assumed lower bound on |B|.
∎
We shall also use the elementary estimate \vartheta_{d,q,k}\leq d(q-1)q^{-k}, which follows from (1+x)^{-d}\geq 1-dx for x\geq 0.
Consequently, whenever the matching construction produces a set B with \vartheta_{d,q,k}<|B|/q^{d}\leq 3\vartheta_{d,q,k}, the subspace in Corollary 2.5 has finite-field covering load |B||C|/q^{d}=(|B|/q^{d})q^{k}\leq 3d(q-1).
The layer-to-grid matching that produces such a set B is proved in Proposition 3.6.
3 The weighted full-cube construction
We now construct the vertical lattice and its Boolean weights.
No Boolean vertex is discarded at this stage.
The folded Gaussian identity separates the total weight of the full cube from its distribution among the vertices.
Min-entropy controls the largest vertex weight, while Shannon entropy later controls the total weight discarded when vertices with small weights are removed.
All constants in this section are absolute.
Every o(1) term is a deterministic function of d alone.
We let d\to\infty and put
\tau\coloneqq\frac{1}{2\log d}.
(3.1)
Let \gamma_{\tau}(u)\coloneqq(2\pi\tau)^{-1/2}e^{-u^{2}/(2\tau)} be the one-dimensional Gaussian density of variance \tau, and set P_{\tau}\coloneqq\int_{-1}^{1}\gamma_{\tau}(u)\,\,\mathrm{d}u.
3.1 Folded Gaussian weights and entropy
Set
\displaystyle Z\coloneqq\int_{-1}^{1}e^{-u^{2}/(2\tau)}\,\,\mathrm{d}u=\sqrt{2\pi\tau}\,P_{\tau}\quad\text{and}\quad g(u)\coloneqq Z^{-1}e^{-u^{2}/(2\tau)}\mathbf{1}_{[-1,1]}(u).
Thus g is the density of N(0,\tau) conditioned on [-1,1].
Let X have density g, and define \mathsf{E}\coloneqq\mathbf{1}_{\{X>0\}} and T\coloneqq\mathsf{E}-X.
Then \mathsf{E}\in\{0,1\}, T\in[0,1], and X=\mathsf{E}-T.
The density of T is f below.
Since a regular conditional probability is determined only almost everywhere, we choose the following continuous version of its Bernoulli parameter:
f(t)\coloneqq g(-t)+g(1-t),\quad\text{and}\quad p(t)\coloneqq\frac{g(1-t)}{f(t)}=\mathbb{P}\left[\mathsf{E}=1\mid T=t\right].
(3.2)
For t=(t_{1},\ldots,t_{d})\in[0,1]^{d}, let P_{t} be the product probability measure on \{0,1\}^{d} given by
P_{t}(\varepsilon)\coloneqq\prod_{i=1}^{d}p(t_{i})^{\varepsilon_{i}}(1-p(t_{i}))^{1-\varepsilon_{i}}.
For a one-dimensional density h, write h^{\otimes d}(x)\coloneqq\prod_{i=1}^{d}h(x_{i}) for its d-fold product density, where x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{d})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.
Summing the next pointwise factorization over the Boolean cube gives the folded-Gaussian identity used throughout the vertical construction.
Lemma 3.1.
For every t\in[0,1]^{d} and \varepsilon\in\{0,1\}^{d},
g^{\otimes d}(\varepsilon-t)=f^{\otimes d}(t)P_{t}(\varepsilon).
(3.3)
Consequently,
\sum_{\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}^{d}}\gamma_{\tau}^{\otimes d}(\varepsilon-t)=P_{\tau}^{d}f^{\otimes d}(t).
(3.4)
Moreover,
1-P_{\tau}=O\left(\frac{1}{d\sqrt{\log d}}\right),\quad\text{and}\quad P_{\tau}^{d}=1-o(1).
(3.5)
Proof.
The chosen conditional version gives g(e-t)=f(t)\mathbb{P}\left[\mathsf{E}=e\mid T=t\right] for every t\in[0,1] and e\in\{0,1\}.
Taking products proves (3.3), and summing over the Boolean cube and using \sum_{\varepsilon}P_{t}(\varepsilon)=1 gives \sum_{\varepsilon}g^{\otimes d}(\varepsilon-t)=f^{\otimes d}(t).
Since g(u)=P_{\tau}^{-1}\gamma_{\tau}(u) for |u|\leq 1, this proves (3.4).
Finally, Mills’ inequality [14] at \tau^{-1/2}=\sqrt{2\log d} gives the first estimate in (3.5); the second follows from d(1-P_{\tau})=O((\log d)^{-1/2}).
∎
The next estimates determine the entropy scale used first to choose the finite-field rank and later to choose the vertical dimension.
The binary entropy function is h_{2}(u)\coloneqq-u\log u-(1-u)\log(1-u) for u\in[0,1].
Define the one-coordinate Shannon entropy and one-coordinate min-entropy, respectively, by
h_{\mathrm{Ber}}(t)\coloneqq h_{2}(p(t)),\quad\text{and}\quad h_{\mathrm{Ber},\infty}(t)\coloneqq-\log\max\{p(t),1-p(t)\}.
(3.6)
For T with density f, put s\coloneqq\mathbb{E}h_{\mathrm{Ber}}(T) and s_{\infty}\coloneqq\mathbb{E}h_{\mathrm{Ber},\infty}(T).
Lemma 3.2.
As d\to\infty,
\displaystyle s
\displaystyle=(2\sqrt{\pi}+o(1))\frac{d^{-1/4}}{\sqrt{\log d}},
(3.7)
\displaystyle s_{\infty}
\displaystyle=\left(\frac{2\pi-4}{\sqrt{\pi}}+o(1)\right)\frac{d^{-1/4}}{\sqrt{\log d}}.
In particular,
ds\asymp ds_{\infty}\asymp\frac{d^{3/4}}{\sqrt{\log d}}\gg\log d.
(3.8)
Proof.
Put t\coloneqq\frac{1}{2}+\tau y.
Directly from (3.2),
p(t)=\frac{e^{y}}{1+e^{y}},\quad\text{and}\quad h_{\mathrm{Ber},\infty}(t)=\log(1+e^{-|y|}).
(3.9)
The same substitution, including the Jacobian \,\mathrm{d}t=\tau\,\,\mathrm{d}y, gives
f\left(\frac{1}{2}+\tau y\right)\tau=\frac{2\tau e^{-1/(8\tau)}}{Z}e^{-\tau y^{2}/2}\cosh(y/2).
For \psi(y)\coloneqq h_{2}(e^{y}/(1+e^{y})) and \psi_{\infty}(y)\coloneqq\log(1+e^{-|y|}), we therefore have
\mathbb{E}\psi_{\star}\left(\frac{T-1/2}{\tau}\right)=\frac{2\tau e^{-1/(8\tau)}}{Z}\int_{-1/(2\tau)}^{1/(2\tau)}e^{-\tau y^{2}/2}\cosh(y/2)\psi_{\star}(y)\,\,\mathrm{d}y,
(3.10)
for \psi_{\star}\in\{\psi,\psi_{\infty}\}.
Extend each integrand by zero outside the interval [-1/(2\tau),1/(2\tau)].
The resulting functions on \mathbb{R} are bounded by the fixed integrable function C(1+|y|)e^{-|y|/2}, uniformly in \tau.
Dominated convergence therefore reduces the leading constants to two one-dimensional integrals, which we now evaluate explicitly.
Both \psi and \psi_{\infty} are even.
For y\geq 0, set x\coloneqq e^{-y}.
Then
\psi(y)=\log(1+x)-\frac{x\log x}{1+x},\quad\text{and}\quad\psi_{\infty}(y)=\log(1+x),\quad\text{and}\quad\cosh(y/2)=\frac{1+x}{2\sqrt{x}}.
It follows that
\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}\cosh(y/2)\psi(y)\,\,\mathrm{d}y=A+B+C\quad\text{and}\quad\int_{\mathbb{R}}\cosh(y/2)\psi_{\infty}(y)\,\,\mathrm{d}y=A+B,
where
A\coloneqq\int_{0}^{1}x^{-3/2}\log(1+x)\,\,\mathrm{d}x,\quad B\coloneqq\int_{0}^{1}x^{-1/2}\log(1+x)\,\,\mathrm{d}x,\quad\text{and}\quad C\coloneqq-\int_{0}^{1}x^{-1/2}\log x\,\,\mathrm{d}x.
For A, perform integration by parts first on [\varepsilon,1] and then let \varepsilon\downarrow 0; the boundary term at \varepsilon tends to zero.
This justification, followed by x=u^{2} for B, gives
\displaystyle A
\displaystyle=-2\log 2+2\int_{0}^{1}\frac{x^{-1/2}}{1+x}\,\,\mathrm{d}x=\pi-2\log 2,
\displaystyle B
\displaystyle=2\int_{0}^{1}\log(1+u^{2})\,\,\mathrm{d}u=2\left[u\log(1+u^{2})-2u+2\arctan u\right]_{u=0}^{u=1}=2\log 2-4+\pi.
Finally, differentiating \int_{0}^{1}x^{a-1}\,\,\mathrm{d}x=a^{-1} at a=1/2 gives C=4.
Consequently,
\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}\cosh(y/2)\psi(y)\,\,\mathrm{d}y=A+B+C=2\pi\quad\text{and}\quad\int_{\mathbb{R}}\cosh(y/2)\psi_{\infty}(y)\,\,\mathrm{d}y=A+B=2\pi-4.
Since Z=\sqrt{2\pi\tau}(1+o(1)), e^{-1/(8\tau)}=d^{-1/4}, and \sqrt{2\tau/\pi}=1/\sqrt{\pi\log d}, substituting these values into (3.10) proves the result.
∎
For a finite probability distribution q, its Shannon entropy and min-entropy are H(q)\coloneqq-\sum_{x}q(x)\log q(x) and H_{\infty}(q)\coloneqq-\log\max_{x}q(x), respectively.
For the product distribution above,
H(P_{t})=\sum_{i=1}^{d}h_{\mathrm{Ber}}(t_{i}),\quad\text{and}\quad H_{\infty}(P_{t})=\sum_{i=1}^{d}h_{\mathrm{Ber},\infty}(t_{i}).
We will use these entropies pointwise on most base points.
The next lemma shows that both remain close to their means with probability at least 1-O(d^{-30}).
Lemma 3.3.
There is an absolute constant C_{\mathrm{ent}}>0 such that, for all sufficiently large d,
\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left[H(P_{T})>ds+C_{\mathrm{ent}}\sqrt{ds\log d}\right]\leq d^{-30}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathbb{P}\left[H_{\infty}(P_{T})<ds_{\infty}-C_{\mathrm{ent}}\sqrt{ds_{\infty}\log d}\right]\leq d^{-30},
where T\coloneqq(T_{1},\ldots,T_{d}) has density f^{\otimes d}.
Proof.
Both functions in (3.6) take values in [0,\log 2].
Hence \Var(h_{\mathrm{Ber}}(T))\leq\mathbb{E}h_{\mathrm{Ber}}(T)^{2}\leq(\log 2)s, and similarly \Var(h_{\mathrm{Ber},\infty}(T))\leq(\log 2)s_{\infty}.
For s_{\star}\in\{s,s_{\infty}\}, put t_{\star}\coloneqq C_{\mathrm{ent}}\sqrt{ds_{\star}\log d}.
Bernstein’s inequality bounds the relevant upper or lower tail by
\exp\left(-\frac{t_{\star}^{2}}{2d(\log 2)s_{\star}+\frac{2}{3}(\log 2)t_{\star}}\right).
By (3.8), ds_{\star}\gg\log d, so t_{\star}=o(ds_{\star}) and the exponent is at most -cC_{\mathrm{ent}}^{2}\log d.
A sufficiently large absolute choice of C_{\mathrm{ent}} makes both probabilities at most d^{-30}.
∎
3.2 A movable information layer
For a probability density \varphi, its differential entropy is h(\varphi)\coloneqq-\int\varphi(x)\log\varphi(x)\,\,\mathrm{d}x whenever this integral is finite.
Set a(t)\coloneqq-\log f(t), so that h(f)=\mathbb{E}a(T).
The Berry–Esseen theorem is a quantitative form of the central limit theorem: when the variance stays bounded away from zero and the third absolute moment is bounded, the distribution function of a normalized sum of d independent copies differs from the standard normal distribution function by O(d^{-1/2}) [25, Chapter V].
We use this estimate to show that a fixed-width information interval has probability of order d^{-1/2}, uniformly when its location is shifted by O(\log d).
The next lemma records the moment bounds needed for this application.
Lemma 3.4.
One has
\displaystyle h(f)
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{\pi e}{\log d}+O\left(\frac{d^{-1/4}}{\sqrt{\log d}}\right),
(3.11)
\displaystyle\Var(a(T))
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}+o(1),
(3.12)
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}|a(T)-h(f)|^{3}
\displaystyle\leq C.
(3.13)
Proof.
We first bound the moments of the conditional-information term, then compare a(T) with U^{2}/2 to obtain the variance and third moment, and finally compute the mean by the mixed entropy chain rule.
For t\in[0,1] and e\in\{0,1\}, put i(t,e)\coloneqq-\log\mathbb{P}\left[\mathsf{E}=e\mid T=t\right] and j(t,e)\coloneqq-\log g(e-t).
The pointwise factorization gives a(T)+i(T,\mathsf{E})=j(T,\mathsf{E}), while the Gaussian form of g gives
a(T)=\log Z+\frac{X^{2}}{2\tau}-i(T,\mathsf{E}).
(3.14)
We first quantify the moments of the conditional-information term.
Let Y\coloneqq(T-1/2)/\tau, I\coloneqq i(T,\mathsf{E}), and p_{y}\coloneqq e^{y}/(1+e^{y}).
For q\in\{1,2,3\}, define m_{q}(y)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}[I^{q}\mid Y=y].
For y\geq 0, the logistic formula (3.9) gives
\displaystyle m_{q}(y)=p_{y}\bigl(\log(1+e^{-y})\bigr)^{q}+(1-p_{y})\bigl(\log(1+e^{y})\bigr)^{q}\leq e^{-qy}+e^{-y}(y+\log 2)^{q}\leq C_{q}(1+y^{q})e^{-y}.
Interchanging the two Bernoulli outcomes shows that m_{q} is even, so
m_{q}(y)\leq C_{q}(1+|y|^{q})e^{-|y|}\quad\text{for }y\in\mathbb{R}.
(3.15)
The density computation in (3.10) now gives the exact representation
\mathbb{E}I^{q}=c_{\tau}\int_{-1/(2\tau)}^{1/(2\tau)}e^{-\tau y^{2}/2}\cosh(y/2)m_{q}(y)\,\,\mathrm{d}y,\quad\text{where}\quad c_{\tau}\coloneqq\frac{2\tau e^{-1/(8\tau)}}{Z}.
By (3.15), the integral is at most
C_{q}\int_{\mathbb{R}}(1+|y|^{q})e^{-|y|/2}\,\,\mathrm{d}y<\infty.
Moreover,
c_{\tau}\asymp\frac{d^{-1/4}}{\sqrt{\log d}}\asymp s
by (3.5), (3.1), and (3.7).
Hence
\mathbb{E}I^{q}=O(s)\quad\text{for }q=1,2,3.
(3.16)
For q=1, this expectation is the conditional entropy H(\mathsf{E}\mid T)=s.
We next record the required truncated-Gaussian moment bounds.
If G\sim N(0,1), then U\coloneqq X/\sqrt{\tau} has the law of G conditioned on |G|\leq\alpha_{d}, where \alpha_{d}\coloneqq\tau^{-1/2}=\sqrt{2\log d}.
For every fixed even q\geq 2, integration by parts yields
\displaystyle\int_{\alpha}^{\infty}x^{q}\gamma_{1}(x)\,\,\mathrm{d}x=\alpha^{q-1}\gamma_{1}(\alpha)+(q-1)\int_{\alpha}^{\infty}x^{q-2}\gamma_{1}(x)\,\,\mathrm{d}x.
Induction in q, starting from Mills’ inequality [14], therefore gives
\mathbb{E}\left[|G|^{q}\mathbf{1}_{\{|G|>\alpha_{d}\}}\right]=O_{q}\left(\frac{(\log d)^{(q-1)/2}}{d}\right)\quad\text{for }q=2,4,6.
Since \mathbb{P}\left[|G|\leq\alpha_{d}\right]=P_{\tau}=1-o(1), division by P_{\tau} in the conditional moments gives
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}U^{2}
\displaystyle=1+O\left(\frac{\sqrt{\log d}}{d}\right),
(3.17)
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}U^{4}
\displaystyle=3+O\left(\frac{(\log d)^{3/2}}{d}\right),
(3.18)
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}U^{6}
\displaystyle=15+O\left(\frac{(\log d)^{5/2}}{d}\right).
Set V\coloneqq U^{2}/2.
The additive constant in (3.14) does not affect variance, so \Var(a(T))=\Var(V-I).
Equations (3.18) and (3.16) imply
\lVert V-\mathbb{E}V\rVert_{2}=O(1),\quad\text{and}\quad\lVert I-\mathbb{E}I\rVert_{2}\leq 2\lVert I\rVert_{2}=O(\sqrt{s}).
Expanding the variance and applying Cauchy–Schwarz to the covariance term, we obtain
\displaystyle\left|\Var(V-I)-\Var(V)\right|
\displaystyle\leq\Var(I)+2|\operatorname{Cov}(V,I)|
\displaystyle\leq\lVert I-\mathbb{E}I\rVert_{2}^{2}+2\lVert V-\mathbb{E}V\rVert_{2}\lVert I-\mathbb{E}I\rVert_{2}=O(s)+O(\sqrt{s})=o(1).
On the other hand, (3.17) and (3.18) give \Var(V)=\frac{1}{4}(\mathbb{E}U^{4}-(\mathbb{E}U^{2})^{2})=\frac{1}{2}+o(1).
Consequently, \Var(a(T))=\frac{1}{2}+o(1), as asserted in (3.12).
The sixth-moment estimate and (3.16) give
\displaystyle\lVert V-\mathbb{E}V\rVert_{3}\leq 2\lVert V\rVert_{3}=2\left(\frac{\mathbb{E}|U|^{6}}{8}\right)^{1/3}=O(1)\quad\text{and}\quad\lVert I-\mathbb{E}I\rVert_{3}\leq 2\lVert I\rVert_{3}=O(s^{1/3}).
Minkowski’s inequality applied to a(T)-h(f)=(V-\mathbb{E}V)-(I-\mathbb{E}I) now yields
\bigl(\mathbb{E}|a(T)-h(f)|^{3}\bigr)^{1/3}\leq\lVert V-\mathbb{E}V\rVert_{3}+\lVert I-\mathbb{E}I\rVert_{3}=O(1),
which proves (3.13).
It remains to compute the mean.
By (3.5), |\log P_{\tau}|=O(1/(d\sqrt{\log d})), while (3.17) controls the quadratic term.
Thus
h(g)=\log Z+\frac{\mathbb{E}U^{2}}{2}=\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi\tau)+\log P_{\tau}+\frac{\mathbb{E}U^{2}}{2}=\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi e\tau){}+O\left(\frac{\sqrt{\log d}}{d}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi e\tau)+o(s),
where the last equality uses (3.7).
Away from the null point X=0, the map X\mapsto(T,\mathsf{E}) is one-to-one on each of the two half-intervals and has Jacobian one.
Splitting the entropy integral over these two branches gives
h(g)=-\int_{0}^{1}f(t)\bigl[(1-p(t))\log\bigl(f(t)(1-p(t))\bigr)+p(t)\log\bigl(f(t)p(t)\bigr)\bigr]\,\,\mathrm{d}t=h(f)+\int_{0}^{1}f(t)h_{2}(p(t))\,\,\mathrm{d}t.
This is the mixed discrete–continuous entropy chain rule in the present setting, so h(g)=h(f)+H(\mathsf{E}\mid T)=h(f)+s, and hence
h(f)=\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi e\tau)-s+o(s)=\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{\pi e}{\log d}+O\left(\frac{d^{-1/4}}{\sqrt{\log d}}\right),
which is (3.11).
∎
For the finite-field step, we need to move the information window by O(\log d) without changing its order of size.
The moment bounds above and the Berry–Esseen theorem give this uniformly in the offset.
Proposition 3.5.
There are absolute constants W,c_{0},C_{0},R_{0}>0 such that the following holds for all sufficiently large d.
For every r\in[-R_{0}\log d,R_{0}\log d], let the information layer \mathcal{G}(r) be the set of all t\in[0,1]^{d} satisfying
\displaystyle dh(f)+r
\displaystyle\leq-\log f^{\otimes d}(t)\leq dh(f)+r+W,
(3.19)
\displaystyle H_{\infty}(P_{t})
\displaystyle\geq ds_{\infty}-C_{\mathrm{ent}}\sqrt{ds_{\infty}\log d},
(3.20)
\displaystyle H(P_{t})
\displaystyle\leq ds+C_{\mathrm{ent}}\sqrt{ds\log d}.
(3.21)
Then
\frac{c_{0}}{\sqrt{d}}\leq\int_{\mathcal{G}(r)}f^{\otimes d}(t)\,\,\mathrm{d}t\leq\frac{C_{0}}{\sqrt{d}},
(3.22)
and, writing v(r)\coloneqq\operatorname{vol}_{d}(\mathcal{G}(r)),
c_{0}d^{-1/2}e^{dh(f)+r}\leq v(r)\leq C_{0}d^{-1/2}e^{dh(f)+r}.
(3.23)
Proof.
Fix R_{0}\coloneqq 3.
Let A_{d}\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{d}a(T_{i}) and \sigma_{d}^{2}\coloneqq\Var(a(T)).
Although the distribution of a(T) depends on d, the Berry–Esseen bound [25, Chapter V] and Lemma 3.4 give
\sup_{x}\left|\mathbb{P}\left[\frac{A_{d}-dh(f)}{\sigma_{d}\sqrt{d}}\leq x\right]-\Phi_{\mathrm{N}}(x)\right|\leq\frac{C\,\mathbb{E}|a(T)-h(f)|^{3}}{\sigma_{d}^{3}\sqrt{d}}\leq\frac{C_{\mathrm{BE}}}{\sqrt{d}}.
Here \Phi_{\mathrm{N}} is the standard normal distribution function.
The uniform third-moment bound and \sigma_{d}^{2}\to 1/2 show that C_{\mathrm{BE}} is absolute.
Since |r|\leq R_{0}\log d=o(\sqrt{d}), the standard normal density is \gamma_{1}(0)+o(1) uniformly on the interval
\left[\frac{r}{\sigma_{d}\sqrt{d}},\frac{r+W}{\sigma_{d}\sqrt{d}}\right].
Thus its probability is (c_{W}+o(1))/\sqrt{d}, where c_{W}\coloneqq W/\sqrt{\pi}.
Passing from a distribution function to an interval uses two endpoints, so the Berry–Esseen error is at most 2C_{\mathrm{BE}}/\sqrt{d}.
Choose W so that c_{W}>4C_{\mathrm{BE}}.
This gives uniform upper and lower bounds of order d^{-1/2} for the event (3.19).
Removing the two exceptional events in Lemma 3.3 changes its probability by at most 2d^{-30}.
This proves (3.22).
On \mathcal{G}(r), the reciprocal density 1/f^{\otimes d}(t) lies between e^{dh(f)+r} and e^{dh(f)+r+W}.
Integrating this reciprocal with respect to f^{\otimes d}(t)\,\,\mathrm{d}t over \mathcal{G}(r) proves (3.23), after changing the absolute constants.
∎
3.3 Matching a layer to the Kakeya threshold
We next match the continuous layer, the grid size, and the discrete rank.
The strict inequality required by Corollary 2.5 must also survive integer rounding.
Bertrand’s postulate states that, for every integer N\geq 2, there is a prime strictly between N and 2N.
Applying it with N=\lceil d(\log d)^{2}\rceil, and using 2\lceil d(\log d)^{2}\rceil\leq 3d(\log d)^{2} for all sufficiently large d, fix once and for all a prime Q=Q(d) satisfying
d(\log d)^{2}\leq Q\leq 3d(\log d)^{2}.
(3.24)
Partition [0,1)^{d} into the half-open grid cells
\mathcal{Q}_{b}\coloneqq\frac{b}{Q}+[0,Q^{-1})^{d},\quad\text{for }b\in\mathbb{F}_{Q}^{d}.
Here each b\in\mathbb{F}_{Q}^{d} is identified with its standard representative in \{0,\ldots,Q-1\}^{d}.
Proposition 3.6.
There are absolute constants c,C>0 such that, for every sufficiently large d and the prime Q=Q(d) fixed in (3.24), there are r\in[-2\log Q,2\log Q], k\in\{2,\ldots,d-1\}, and B\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{Q}^{d} such that every cell \mathcal{Q}_{b} with b\in B meets \mathcal{G}(r).
With \beta\coloneqq|B|/Q^{d} and \vartheta_{k}\coloneqq\vartheta_{d,Q,k}, one has
\vartheta_{k}<\beta\leq 3\vartheta_{k}
(3.25)
and
c\,v(r)\leq\beta\leq C\,v(r).
(3.26)
Consequently, there is a k-dimensional linear subspace C_{d}\leq\mathbb{F}_{Q}^{d} such that
B+C_{d}=\mathbb{F}_{Q}^{d}
(3.27)
and
c\,dQ\leq\beta Q^{k}=\frac{|B||C_{d}|}{Q^{d}}\leq C\,dQ.
(3.28)
Proof.
We first choose the rank k, then shift the information layer to the corresponding Kakeya threshold, select enough intersecting grid cells, and finally apply Corollary 2.5.
Put v_{*}\coloneqq d^{-1/2}e^{dh(f)} and x_{k}\coloneqq d(Q-1)Q^{-k}.
By (3.11), \log v_{*}=-\frac{d}{2}\log\log d+O(d), whereas x_{2}=d(Q-1)Q^{-2}\geq c/(\log d)^{2} and x_{d-1}\leq\exp(-(1+o(1))d\log d).
Thus, for all sufficiently large d, there is k\in\{2,\ldots,d-1\} such that
x_{k}\leq v_{*}<Qx_{k}.
(3.29)
In particular, x_{k}\to 0.
Moreover, \log(Qv_{*})=-\frac{d}{2}\log\log d+O(d)\to-\infty, so Qx_{k}\leq Qv_{*}\to 0.
Set u_{k}\coloneqq(Q-1)Q^{-k}=x_{k}/d.
Since du_{k}=x_{k}\to 0, the definition (2.2) and the expansion 1-(1+u_{k})^{-d}=du_{k}(1+O(du_{k})), uniform for the selected k, give
\vartheta_{k}=(1+o(1))x_{k}.
(3.30)
Choose a sufficiently large absolute constant M, depending only on the lower constant c_{0} in (3.23), and put
r\coloneqq\log\frac{M\vartheta_{k}}{v_{*}}.
(3.31)
Equations (3.29) and (3.30) imply -\log Q+O(1)\leq r\leq O(1), so r\in[-2\log Q,2\log Q] for large d.
Since \log Q=(1+o(1))\log d, this lies in the range of Proposition 3.5, where R_{0}=3.
By (3.23) and (3.31),
c_{0}M\vartheta_{k}\leq v(r)\leq C_{0}M\vartheta_{k}.
(3.32)
Fix M so that c_{0}M\geq 8.
Let S\coloneqq\{b\in\mathbb{F}_{Q}^{d}\colon\mathcal{Q}_{b}\cap\mathcal{G}(r)\neq\varnothing\}.
The cells are disjoint and cover [0,1)^{d}.
Since \mathcal{G}(r)\setminus[0,1)^{d} lies in the boundary of the cube and hence has zero d-dimensional volume, the union of the cells indexed by S has volume at least v(r).
Therefore
\frac{|S|}{Q^{d}}\geq v(r)\geq 8\vartheta_{k}.
(3.33)
We also have Q^{-d}\leq\vartheta_{k} for all sufficiently large d, uniformly for the selected k.
Indeed, (3.30) and k\leq d-1 give \vartheta_{k}Q^{d}\geq\frac{1}{2}d(Q-1)Q^{d-k}\geq 1.
Choose any subset B\subseteq S of cardinality
|B|=\left\lceil 2\vartheta_{k}Q^{d}\right\rceil.
(3.34)
The choice is possible by (3.33), and the last observation gives
2\vartheta_{k}\leq\beta\leq 2\vartheta_{k}+Q^{-d}\leq 3\vartheta_{k}.
This proves the strict inequality and all rounding assertions in (3.25).
Combining this estimate with (3.32) proves (3.26).
Now apply Corollary 2.5 to obtain a k-dimensional subspace C_{d} satisfying (3.27).
Finally, (3.30) gives \beta Q^{k}\asymp x_{k}Q^{k}=d(Q-1)\asymp dQ, which proves (3.28).
∎
3.4 Construction A and the scaled weighted construction
We lift the covering subspace C_{d} to a Euclidean lattice so that every torus point can be moved into a selected grid cell.
The stability lemma then transfers the information-layer estimates from the chosen representative of that cell to the actual point.
For every b\in B, choose a representative
t_{b}\in\mathcal{G}(r)\cap\mathcal{Q}_{b}.
(3.35)
Let \operatorname{red}_{Q}\colon\mathbb{Z}^{d}\to\mathbb{F}_{Q}^{d} be coordinatewise reduction modulo Q.
Define the unscaled Construction-A lattice by
\Lambda_{0}\coloneqq\frac{1}{Q}\operatorname{red}_{Q}^{-1}(C_{d})=\left\{\frac{z}{Q}\colon z\in\mathbb{Z}^{d},\ \operatorname{red}_{Q}(z)\in C_{d}\right\}.
Equivalently, if \widehat{c}\in\{0,\ldots,Q-1\}^{d} denotes the standard integer representative of c\in C_{d}, then
\Lambda_{0}=\mathbb{Z}^{d}+\left\{\frac{\widehat{c}}{Q}\colon c\in C_{d}\right\}.
Changing the integer representative of c only adds an element of \mathbb{Z}^{d}, so the lattice is independent of this choice.
Since \Lambda_{0}/\mathbb{Z}^{d}\cong C_{d}, its covolume is
\det\Lambda_{0}=|C_{d}|^{-1}=Q^{-k}.
(3.36)
This is the usual Construction-A lift of a linear code, as used, for example, by Erez, Litsyn, and Zamir [10].
To pass from a selected point of a good grid cell to every point in that cell, we need the following stability estimate.
Lemma 3.7.
If t,t^{\prime}\in[0,1]^{d} and \lVert t-t^{\prime}\rVert_{\infty}\leq Q^{-1}, then
\displaystyle\left|\log f^{\otimes d}(t)-\log f^{\otimes d}(t^{\prime})\right|
\displaystyle\leq\Delta_{d},
(3.37)
\displaystyle|H(P_{t})-H(P_{t^{\prime}})|+|H_{\infty}(P_{t})-H_{\infty}(P_{t^{\prime}})|
\displaystyle\leq C\Delta_{d},
(3.38)
where
\Delta_{d}\coloneqq\frac{d}{Q\tau}=O\left(\frac{1}{\log d}\right).
(3.39)
Proof.
The two Gaussian summands defining f give |(\log f)^{\prime}(u)|\leq\tau^{-1} for 0<u<1, with the corresponding one-sided bounds at the endpoints.
Thus the mean-value theorem proves (3.37).
In the logistic coordinate y=(t-1/2)/\tau, the function h_{2}(e^{y}/(1+e^{y})) has bounded derivative.
The function \log(1+e^{-|y|}) is not differentiable at zero, but its two one-sided derivatives are bounded in absolute value; hence it is globally Lipschitz.
Applying these Lipschitz bounds coordinatewise proves (3.38).
The estimate (3.39) follows from (3.1) and (3.24).
∎
Passing to standard-Gaussian coordinates scales \Lambda_{0} by \tau^{-1/2} and hence multiplies its covolume by \tau^{-d/2}.
Define the scaled vertical lattice and the scaling map by
\Lambda_{v}\coloneqq\tau^{-1/2}\Lambda_{0},\quad\text{and}\quad\Psi_{d}\coloneqq\tau^{-1/2}\operatorname{Id}_{d}.
(3.40)
Then \Psi_{d}(\mathbb{Z}^{d})\subseteq\Lambda_{v} is a finite-index full-rank sublattice, and
\det\Lambda_{v}=\tau^{-d/2}\det\Lambda_{0}=\tau^{-d/2}Q^{-k}.
(3.41)
The next proposition is the output of the vertical construction.
It places a full Boolean pattern above every vertical translate and records its total Gaussian weight, largest normalized weight, and entropy.
Proposition 3.8.
For all sufficiently large d, the lattice \Lambda_{v} defined in (3.40) has the following property.
For every y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, there are \lambda_{y}\in\Lambda_{v} and \widetilde{t}_{y}\in[0,1)^{d} such that
y-\lambda_{y}-\Psi_{d}(\varepsilon)=\frac{\widetilde{t}_{y}-\varepsilon}{\sqrt{\tau}}\qquad\text{for every }\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}^{d}.
(3.42)
Define the vertex weights and their total weight by
\mathsf{w}_{y,\varepsilon}\coloneqq\det\Lambda_{v}\,\gamma_{d}\left(y-\lambda_{y}-\Psi_{d}(\varepsilon)\right),\quad\text{and}\quad\mathsf{W}_{y}\coloneqq\sum_{\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}^{d}}\mathsf{w}_{y,\varepsilon}.
Uniformly in y,
\displaystyle\mathsf{W}_{y}
\displaystyle=d^{-5/2+o(1)},
(3.43)
\displaystyle\frac{\max_{\varepsilon}\mathsf{w}_{y,\varepsilon}}{\mathsf{W}_{y}}
\displaystyle\leq\exp\left(-ds_{\infty}+C\sqrt{ds_{\infty}\log d}+o(\log d)\right),
(3.44)
\displaystyle-\sum_{\varepsilon}\frac{\mathsf{w}_{y,\varepsilon}}{\mathsf{W}_{y}}\log\frac{\mathsf{w}_{y,\varepsilon}}{\mathsf{W}_{y}}
\displaystyle\leq ds+C\sqrt{ds\log d}+o(\log d).
(3.45)
Here the first estimate is uniform in the following explicit sense: there is an absolute constant C_{\xi}>0 such that one may take \xi_{d}\coloneqq C_{\xi}\log\log d/\log d and obtain d^{-5/2-\xi_{d}}\leq\mathsf{W}_{y}\leq d^{-5/2+\xi_{d}} for every y.
All points in (3.42) have norm at most
\sqrt{\frac{d}{\tau}}=\sqrt{2d\log d}.
(3.46)
Proof.
We first use B+C_{d}=\mathbb{F}_{Q}^{d} to move the given point into a selected cell, then derive exact formulas for the Boolean weights, and finally transfer the information-layer bounds by cell stability.
Fix y\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and put w\coloneqq\sqrt{\tau}\,y.
Choose z_{0}\in\mathbb{Z}^{d} such that w-z_{0}\in[0,1)^{d}, and set w_{0}\coloneqq w-z_{0}.
Let z\in\mathbb{F}_{Q}^{d} be the index of the cell containing w_{0}, let \widehat{z} be its standard integer representative, and write w_{0}=\widehat{z}/Q+u with u\in[0,Q^{-1})^{d}.
By (3.27), write z=b+c in \mathbb{F}_{Q}^{d}, where b\in B and c\in C_{d}.
If \widehat{b} and \widehat{c} are the standard integer representatives, there is a \kappa\in\mathbb{Z}^{d} such that \widehat{z}=\widehat{b}+\widehat{c}-Q\kappa.
Then
\widetilde{t}_{y}\coloneqq w_{0}-\frac{\widehat{c}}{Q}+\kappa=\frac{\widehat{b}}{Q}+u\in\mathcal{Q}_{b}.
(3.47)
Thus, with
\lambda_{0}\coloneqq z_{0}-\kappa+\frac{\widehat{c}}{Q}\in\Lambda_{0},\quad\text{and}\quad\lambda_{y}\coloneqq\tau^{-1/2}\lambda_{0},
one has \widetilde{t}_{y}=w-\lambda_{0}, which proves (3.42).
Equation (3.46) follows because every coordinate of \widetilde{t}_{y}-\varepsilon lies in [-1,1].
The determinant scaling in (3.41) gives the exact identity
\displaystyle\mathsf{w}_{y,\varepsilon}
\displaystyle=\det\Lambda_{0}\,\gamma_{\tau}^{\otimes d}(\widetilde{t}_{y}-\varepsilon),
\displaystyle\mathsf{W}_{y}
\displaystyle=\det\Lambda_{0}\,P_{\tau}^{d}f^{\otimes d}(\widetilde{t}_{y}),
(3.48)
\displaystyle\frac{\mathsf{w}_{y,\varepsilon}}{\mathsf{W}_{y}}
\displaystyle=P_{\widetilde{t}_{y}}(\varepsilon).
(3.49)
Here the second and third lines follow from Lemma 3.1.
Thus the factor \tau^{d/2} arising from the Gaussian scaling is incorporated exactly through (3.41).
By (3.35) and (3.47), \lVert\widetilde{t}_{y}-t_{b}\rVert_{\infty}\leq Q^{-1}.
Equations (3.19) and (3.37) therefore give
f^{\otimes d}(\widetilde{t}_{y})=\exp\bigl(-dh(f)-r+O(W+\Delta_{d})\bigr).
On the other hand, (3.34), (3.31), and v_{*}=d^{-1/2}e^{dh(f)} give
\beta f^{\otimes d}(\widetilde{t}_{y})=d^{-1/2}\exp(O(W+\Delta_{d})).
(3.50)
Combining (3.28), (3.36), (3.50), and (3.48), we obtain, uniformly in y,
\mathsf{W}_{y}=P_{\tau}^{d}Q^{-k}f^{\otimes d}(\widetilde{t}_{y})=d^{-3/2}Q^{-1}e^{O(1)}=d^{-5/2}(\log d)^{-2}e^{O(1)}.
Here we used P_{\tau}^{d}=1-o(1) and Q\asymp d(\log d)^{2}.
This proves (3.43), and choosing C_{\xi} sufficiently large gives the explicit two-sided bound in the statement.
Finally, (3.20), (3.21), and Lemma 3.7 yield
\displaystyle H_{\infty}(P_{\widetilde{t}_{y}})\geq ds_{\infty}-C_{\mathrm{ent}}\sqrt{ds_{\infty}\log d}-C\Delta_{d}\quad\text{and}\quad H(P_{\widetilde{t}_{y}})\leq ds+C_{\mathrm{ent}}\sqrt{ds\log d}+C\Delta_{d}.
Since \Delta_{d}=o(\log d), the exact normalized law (3.49) proves (3.44) and (3.45).
∎
4 Sections of varying volume and weighted lifting
The vertical construction assigns a different Gaussian weight to each Boolean vertex.
Equalizing the corresponding horizontal sections would lose this information.
In this section we retain the volume of each section, find one horizontal lattice for all loads in a prescribed window, amplify label-dependent hole bounds, and insert the resulting shifts into a finite-index shear.
The determinant of the final lattice is the product of the horizontal determinant and that of the scaled vertical lattice.
4.1 Discretizing sections of varying volume
Let K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} be a convex body.
After an invertible affine transformation, assume that the uniform probability measure on K is isotropic.
Fix an integer d<n, put m\coloneqq n-d, and let \mathbb{R}^{n}=E\oplus F be an orthogonal decomposition, with \dim E=m and \dim F=d, supplied by Theorem 2.3.
For y\in F, write K_{y}\coloneqq\{x\in E\colon x+y\in K\}.
For the uniform measure on K, the definition of \rho_{F} gives \rho_{F}(y)=\operatorname{vol}_{m}(K_{y})/\operatorname{vol}_{n}(K).
For F supplied by Theorem 2.3 and all sufficiently large n, so that Cn^{-c_{3}}<1, the lower bound in (2.1) is positive at every point of the open ball \{\lVert y\rVert_{2}<n^{c_{4}}\}.
Each such point therefore belongs to the support of the marginal, which is P_{F}(K).
Thus the entire open ball is contained in P_{F}(K), and, because the ball is open, each of its points lies in \operatorname{int}(P_{F}(K)).
Consequently, throughout this range,
\operatorname{vol}_{m}(K_{y})=\bigl(1+O(n^{-c_{3}})\bigr)\operatorname{vol}_{n}(K)\gamma_{d}(y).
(4.1)
The horizontal sections vary continuously with y, but the later union bound requires a finite family.
The next proposition replaces all sections in the relevant ball by at most (Cm^{2})^{d} slightly smaller model sections while preserving their volumes up to a factor 1+O(m^{-1}).
Proposition 4.1.
There is an absolute constant C>0 with the following property.
Let m\coloneqq n-d, suppose that m\geq 2 and d\leq n^{c_{1}}, and let R>0 satisfy
2dR<n^{c_{4}}.
(4.2)
For all sufficiently large n, every convex body K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} has an affine image \widetilde{K} and an orthogonal decomposition \mathbb{R}^{n}=E\oplus F, with \dim E=m and \dim F=d.
For s>0, write B_{s}^{F}\coloneqq\{y\in F\colon\lVert y\rVert_{2}\leq s\}, and use \gamma_{d}(y)\coloneqq(2\pi)^{-d/2}e^{-\lVert y\rVert_{2}^{2}/2} for the standard Gaussian density on F.
Define \widetilde{K}_{y}\coloneqq\{x\in E\colon x+y\in\widetilde{K}\}.
There are convex bodies J_{1},\ldots,J_{N}\subseteq E, with N\leq(Cm^{2})^{d}, such that the following holds.
For every y\in B_{R}^{F}, there is an a\in[N] satisfying
\displaystyle J_{a}
\displaystyle\subseteq\widetilde{K}_{y},
(4.3)
\displaystyle\left(1-\frac{1}{m^{2}}\right)^{2m}\operatorname{vol}_{m}(\widetilde{K}_{y})
\displaystyle\leq\operatorname{vol}_{m}(J_{a})\leq\operatorname{vol}_{m}(\widetilde{K}_{y}).
(4.4)
In particular, the label a can be chosen so that, uniformly in y,
\operatorname{vol}_{m}(J_{a})=\left(1+O\left(\frac{1}{m}+n^{-c_{3}}\right)\right)\operatorname{vol}_{n}(\widetilde{K})\gamma_{d}(y).
(4.5)
Proof.
We first center all sections over a containing simplex by a determinant-one shear, then choose a fine net in the target ball, and finally contract the net sections so that they lie in every nearby section.
Let K_{0} be an affine image of K whose uniform probability measure is isotropic.
Choose F for K_{0} from Theorem 2.3, and set E\coloneqq F^{\perp}.
Let \Sigma\subseteq F be a regular d-simplex centered at the origin and having inradius 2R.
The circumradius of a regular d-simplex is d times its inradius, so B_{2R}^{F}\subseteq\Sigma\subseteq B_{2dR}^{F}.
Since 2dR<n^{c_{4}}, the support conclusion above gives \Sigma\subseteq\operatorname{int}(P_{F}(K_{0})).
Moreover, (4.1) shows that every vertex section has positive m-dimensional volume.
Let v_{0},\ldots,v_{d} be the vertices of \Sigma, and choose x_{i}\in(K_{0})_{v_{i}}.
Write
y=\sum_{i=0}^{d}\alpha_{i}(y)v_{i},\quad\text{where}\quad\sum_{i=0}^{d}\alpha_{i}(y)=1,
where the \alpha_{i}(y) are the affine barycentric coordinates of y, and define x_{0}(y)\coloneqq\sum_{i=0}^{d}\alpha_{i}(y)x_{i}.
For y\in\Sigma, all the coefficients are nonnegative, and convexity gives x_{0}(y)\in(K_{0})_{y}.
Apply the affine shear \mathcal{S}(x,y)\coloneqq(x-x_{0}(y),y), and set \widetilde{K}\coloneqq\mathcal{S}(K_{0}).
The linear part of \mathcal{S} is block triangular with determinant one, and the shear preserves the vertical marginal and every section volume.
We therefore have
0\in\widetilde{K}_{y}\qquad\text{for every }y\in\Sigma.
(4.6)
Choose an R/m^{2}-net \mathcal{Y}\coloneqq\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{N}\}\subseteq B_{R}^{F}.
The standard packing estimate gives
N\leq\left(1+\frac{2R}{R/m^{2}}\right)^{d}=(1+2m^{2})^{d}\leq(Cm^{2})^{d}.
Fix y\in B_{R}^{F}, and choose y_{a}\in\mathcal{Y} with \lVert y-y_{a}\rVert_{2}\leq R/m^{2}.
If y=y_{a}, the two inclusions below hold with \sigma\coloneqq 0.
Otherwise, set
u\coloneqq\frac{y-y_{a}}{\lVert y-y_{a}\rVert_{2}},\quad\text{and}\quad\sigma\coloneqq\frac{\lVert y-y_{a}\rVert_{2}}{R}\leq\frac{1}{m^{2}},
and define z_{+}\coloneqq y_{a}+Ru and z_{-}\coloneqq y-Ru.
Both z_{+} and z_{-} belong to B_{2R}^{F}\subseteq\Sigma, and
y=(1-\sigma)y_{a}+\sigma z_{+},\quad\text{and}\quad y_{a}=(1-\sigma)y+\sigma z_{-}.
Convexity of \widetilde{K}, together with (4.6), gives, in either case,
(1-\sigma)\widetilde{K}_{y_{a}}\subseteq\widetilde{K}_{y},\quad\text{and}\quad(1-\sigma)\widetilde{K}_{y}\subseteq\widetilde{K}_{y_{a}}.
For every a\in[N], define
J_{a}\coloneqq\left(1-\frac{1}{m^{2}}\right)\widetilde{K}_{y_{a}},
(4.7)
where the contraction is about the origin.
By (4.6), 0\in\widetilde{K}_{y_{a}}.
For any convex set C containing the origin, rC\subseteq sC whenever 0\leq r\leq s.
Since 1-m^{-2}\leq 1-\sigma, we therefore have J_{a}\subseteq(1-\sigma)\widetilde{K}_{y_{a}}\subseteq\widetilde{K}_{y}, which proves (4.3).
The second inclusion gives
\operatorname{vol}_{m}(\widetilde{K}_{y_{a}})\geq(1-\sigma)^{m}\operatorname{vol}_{m}(\widetilde{K}_{y})\geq\left(1-\frac{1}{m^{2}}\right)^{m}\operatorname{vol}_{m}(\widetilde{K}_{y}).
Multiplying by the volume contraction in (4.7) proves the lower bound in (4.4); its upper bound follows from (4.3).
Finally, (1-m^{-2})^{2m}=1+O(m^{-1}), and (4.1) proves (4.5).
∎
4.2 A common horizontal lattice and simultaneous shifts
The next lemma applies the Rogers–Schmidt estimate to all model sections at once.
The sections may have different volumes; only their individual loads enter the union bound.
Lemma 4.2.
Let m be sufficiently large, let D_{h}>0, and let J_{a}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m}, a\in\mathcal{A}, be finitely many compact sets of positive volume.
Define the load of J_{a} by u_{a}\coloneqq\operatorname{vol}_{m}(J_{a})/D_{h}, and suppose u_{a}\leq\eta_{m} for every a\in\mathcal{A}.
Let 0<c<1.
If
(1+c_{\mathrm{RS}})\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}e^{-(1-c)u_{a}}<1,
(4.8)
then there exists a lattice \Lambda_{h}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m}, with \det\Lambda_{h}=D_{h}, such that
\bar{\rho}(\Lambda_{h}+J_{a})\leq e^{-cu_{a}}\qquad\text{for every }a\in\mathcal{A}.
(4.9)
In particular, if |\mathcal{A}|\leq N and T\leq u_{a}\leq\eta_{m} for every a\in\mathcal{A}, then the conclusion with c=1/2 holds whenever
T\geq 2\log\bigl(2(1+c_{\mathrm{RS}})N\bigr).
(4.10)
Proof.
For a\in\mathcal{A}, the rescaled set \widetilde{J}_{a}\coloneqq D_{h}^{-1/m}J_{a} has volume u_{a}.
For a Haar–Siegel random unimodular lattice L, Theorem 2.1 and u_{a}\leq\eta_{m} give
\mathbb{E}_{L}\bar{\rho}(L+\widetilde{J}_{a})\leq e^{-u_{a}}+c_{\mathrm{RS}}e^{-\eta_{m}}\leq(1+c_{\mathrm{RS}})e^{-u_{a}}.
Markov’s inequality therefore gives
\mathbb{P}_{L}\left[\bar{\rho}(L+\widetilde{J}_{a})>e^{-cu_{a}}\right]\leq(1+c_{\mathrm{RS}})e^{-(1-c)u_{a}}.
Condition (4.8) and a union bound produce one L for which none of these events occurs.
Taking \Lambda_{h}\coloneqq D_{h}^{1/m}L proves (4.9).
Under (4.10), the left-hand side of (4.8), with c=1/2, is at most 1/2.
∎
The next result chooses shifts that make all relevant labeled Boolean intersections small at the same time.
It will be applied to the horizontal quotient torus.
Let \mathbb{T} be a compact abelian group with Haar probability measure \mu.
Let U_{1},\ldots,U_{N}\subseteq\mathbb{T} be measurable, and suppose \mu(U_{a})\leq\delta_{a}\leq 1, where \delta_{a} may depend on a.
For I\subseteq[d], a labeled pattern consists of a nonempty set P\subseteq\{0,1\}^{I} and a label map \ell\colon P\to[N].
Given a labeled pattern and z_{1},\ldots,z_{d}\in\mathbb{T}, define
\mathcal{U}_{I,P,\ell}(z)\coloneqq\bigcap_{\omega\in P}\left(U_{\ell(\omega)}-\sum_{i\in I}\omega_{i}z_{i}\right).
For j\in I and e\in\{0,1\}, let \iota_{j,e}\colon\{0,1\}^{I\setminus\{j\}}\to\{0,1\}^{I} insert the coordinate e in position j, and define the e-slice
P_{j,e}\coloneqq\bigl\{\omega^{\prime}\in\{0,1\}^{I\setminus\{j\}}\colon\iota_{j,e}(\omega^{\prime})\in P\bigr\}.
When P_{j,e}\neq\varnothing, its induced label map is
\ell_{j,e}(\omega^{\prime})\coloneqq\ell\bigl(\iota_{j,e}(\omega^{\prime})\bigr),\quad\text{for }\omega^{\prime}\in P_{j,e}.
Thus a slice retains the original labels of its surviving Boolean vertices.
A family \mathscr{C} of triples (I,P,\ell) is slice-closed if (I\setminus\{j\},P_{j,e},\ell_{j,e})\in\mathscr{C} whenever (I,P,\ell)\in\mathscr{C}, j\in I, and P_{j,e}\neq\varnothing.
This closure condition is exactly what the coordinate-by-coordinate induction requires: after one Boolean coordinate is fixed, every nonempty slice remains among the patterns controlled at the preceding stage.
Theorem 4.3.
Let \mathscr{C} be a finite slice-closed family of triples (I,P,\ell), allowing both the coordinate set I and the pattern P to vary.
If L\geq 2|\mathscr{C}|, then there are shifts z_{1},\ldots,z_{d}\in\mathbb{T} such that, simultaneously for every (I,P,\ell)\in\mathscr{C},
\mu\bigl(\mathcal{U}_{I,P,\ell}(z)\bigr)\leq L^{|P|-1}\prod_{\omega\in P}\delta_{\ell(\omega)}.
(4.11)
Proof.
If one of the factors on the right of (4.11) is zero, then the intersection on the left is contained in a translate of a null set, so the desired inequality holds for every choice of shifts.
We may therefore consider only triples for which all relevant factors are positive.
For 0\leq q\leq d, let \mathscr{C}_{\leq q}\coloneqq\{(I,P,\ell)\in\mathscr{C}\colon I\subseteq[q]\}.
We choose the shifts inductively so that (4.11) holds for every triple in \mathscr{C}_{\leq q}.
For q=0, every nonempty pattern is a singleton, and the assertion is exactly \mu(U_{a})\leq\delta_{a}.
Suppose that z_{1},\ldots,z_{q-1} have been chosen for \mathscr{C}_{\leq q-1}.
This property will not be affected by the choice of z_{q}, because none of the earlier intersections uses the q-th coordinate.
Consider a triple (I,P,\ell)\in\mathscr{C}_{\leq q} with q\in I, and put I^{\prime}\coloneqq I\setminus\{q\}.
By slice closure, each nonempty q-slice belongs to \mathscr{C}_{\leq q-1}.
If only the e-slice is nonempty, then
\mathcal{U}_{I,P,\ell}(z)=\mathcal{U}_{I^{\prime},P_{q,e},\ell_{q,e}}(z)-ez_{q}.
The two sets have the same measure, |P_{q,e}|=|P|, and the induction hypothesis gives the required bound without any loss.
It remains to treat triples for which both slices are nonempty.
For such a triple, set A\coloneqq\mathcal{U}_{I^{\prime},P_{q,0},\ell_{q,0}}(z) and B\coloneqq\mathcal{U}_{I^{\prime},P_{q,1},\ell_{q,1}}(z).
Then
\mathcal{U}_{I,P,\ell}(z)=A\cap(B-z_{q}).
For Haar-uniform z_{q}, Fubini’s theorem and translation invariance give
\mathbb{E}_{z_{q}}\mu\bigl(A\cap(B-z_{q})\bigr)=\mu(A)\mu(B).
The induction hypothesis bounds the last product by
L^{|P_{q,0}|-1}L^{|P_{q,1}|-1}\prod_{\omega\in P}\delta_{\ell(\omega)}=L^{|P|-2}\prod_{\omega\in P}\delta_{\ell(\omega)}.
Markov’s inequality shows that the target bound fails for this triple with probability at most 1/L.
At most |\mathscr{C}|\leq L/2 triples in \mathscr{C}_{\leq q} have two nonempty q-slices, so the union of their failure events has probability at most 1/2.
We may therefore choose one z_{q} that works for all of them.
This completes the induction.
∎
If \mathscr{A} is a family of labeled patterns in \{0,1\}^{d}, regard each (P,\ell)\in\mathscr{A} as the triple ([d],P,\ell).
Its slice closure, denoted by \operatorname{scl}(\mathscr{A}), is the smallest slice-closed family containing these triples.
The crude family containing every labeled nonempty subpattern on every surviving coordinate set has size at most
\sum_{I\subseteq[d]}(N+1)^{2^{|I|}}\leq 2^{d}(N+1)^{2^{d}}.
Consequently, with \mathscr{C}\coloneqq\operatorname{scl}(\mathscr{A}) and L\coloneqq 2|\mathscr{C}|,
\log L\leq\log 2+d\log 2+2^{d}\log(N+1).
4.3 Finite-index lifting and entropy pruning
We now build the simultaneous shifts into a single lattice.
The finite-index hypothesis is the algebraic bridge: after choosing a basis map B for \Lambda_{v}, the inclusion \Psi(\mathbb{Z}^{d})\subseteq\Lambda_{v} yields a nonsingular integer matrix M such that \Psi=B\circ M.
Since M^{\mathsf{T}} is onto on the horizontal torus, the prescribed shifts can be lifted to shear parameters without changing the product of the horizontal and vertical determinants.
The next theorem formalizes this construction.
Theorem 4.4.
Let \mathbb{R}^{n}=E\oplus F be an orthogonal decomposition with \dim E=m and \dim F=d.
Let K\subseteq E\oplus F be compact, and define its horizontal sections by K_{y}\coloneqq\{x\in E\colon x+y\in K\}.
Suppose that:
(i)
J_{1},\ldots,J_{N}\subseteq E are compact sets, and \Lambda_{h}\subseteq E is a lattice. For each a\in[N], let \delta_{a}\in[0,1] satisfy
\bar{\rho}(\Lambda_{h}+J_{a})\leq\delta_{a}\quad\text{for every }a\in[N];
(ii)
\Lambda_{v}\subseteq F is a lattice, \Psi\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to F is a linear isomorphism, and \Psi(\mathbb{Z}^{d})\subseteq\Lambda_{v} is a finite-index sublattice;
(iii)
\mathscr{A} is a finite family of pairs (P,\ell) with \varnothing\neq P\subseteq\{0,1\}^{d} and \ell\colon P\to[N]; the sets P may have different cardinalities. For every w\in F, there are \lambda\in\Lambda_{v} and (P,\ell)\in\mathscr{A} satisfying
J_{\ell(\omega)}\subseteq K_{w-\lambda-\Psi(\omega)}\qquad\text{for every }\omega\in P.
(4.12)
Let \mathscr{C}\coloneqq\operatorname{scl}(\mathscr{A}) and L\coloneqq 2|\mathscr{C}|.
Then there exists a lattice \Lambda\subseteq E\oplus F such that
\det\Lambda=\det\Lambda_{h}\det\Lambda_{v}
(4.13)
and
\bar{\rho}(\Lambda+K)\leq\max_{(P,\ell)\in\mathscr{A}}L^{|P|-1}\prod_{\omega\in P}\delta_{\ell(\omega)}.
(4.14)
In particular, if c>0, u_{a}\geq 0, and \delta_{a}\leq e^{-cu_{a}} for every a\in[N], then
\log\bar{\rho}(\Lambda+K)\leq\max_{(P,\ell)\in\mathscr{A}}\left((|P|-1)\log L-c\sum_{\omega\in P}u_{\ell(\omega)}\right).
(4.15)
Here and below, \log 0\coloneqq-\infty.
Proof.
Choose a linear isomorphism S\colon E\to\mathbb{R}^{m} satisfying S(\Lambda_{h})=\mathbb{Z}^{m}, apply S\oplus\operatorname{id}_{F} to K and all the J_{a}, and keep the same notation for their images.
The section inclusions and hole proportions are unchanged.
At the end we will apply the inverse map, which multiplies the covolume by |\det(S^{-1})|=\det\Lambda_{h}.
Choose a basis map B\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to F satisfying B(\mathbb{Z}^{d})=\Lambda_{v}.
Since \Psi(\mathbb{Z}^{d})\subseteq\Lambda_{v} has finite index, there is a nonsingular integer matrix M\in M_{d}(\mathbb{Z}) such that \Psi=B\circ M.
Let \mathbb{T}^{m}\coloneqq\mathbb{R}^{m}/\mathbb{Z}^{m}, let \pi\colon\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{T}^{m} be the quotient map, let \mu be Haar probability measure on \mathbb{T}^{m}, and set U_{a}\coloneqq\mathbb{T}^{m}\setminus\pi(J_{a}).
Since J_{a} is compact, U_{a} is Borel, and \mu(U_{a})=\bar{\rho}(\mathbb{Z}^{m}+J_{a})\leq\delta_{a}.
Apply Theorem 4.3 to \mathscr{C}, obtaining shifts z_{1},\ldots,z_{d}\in\mathbb{T}^{m}.
Write z\coloneqq(z_{1},\ldots,z_{d}).
Consider the homomorphism from (\mathbb{T}^{m})^{d} to itself given by
\chi\longmapsto M^{\mathsf{T}}\chi.
This map is onto.
It need not be injective, but Smith normal form reduces surjectivity to the fact that multiplication by a nonzero integer is onto on \mathbb{T}^{m}.
Choose \chi\coloneqq(\chi_{1},\ldots,\chi_{d}) satisfying M^{\mathsf{T}}\chi=z, and choose representatives \widehat{\chi}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}.
For \nu\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}, write \nu\cdot\widehat{\chi}\coloneqq\sum_{j\in[d]}\nu_{j}\widehat{\chi}_{j}.
Define the shear lattice in the normalized coordinates by
\Gamma\coloneqq\bigl\{(k-\nu\cdot\widehat{\chi},B(\nu))\colon k\in\mathbb{Z}^{m},\ \nu\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}\bigr\}.
Its generating matrix is block triangular, with diagonal blocks I_{m} and B, so \det\Gamma=|\det B|=\det\Lambda_{v}.
Let \mathcal{D}_{h}\coloneqq[0,1)^{m}, and let \mathcal{D}_{v} be a half-open fundamental domain for \Lambda_{v}.
To reduce a point (x,w) modulo \Gamma, first choose \nu\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}, uniquely outside a null boundary set, such that w-B(\nu)\in\mathcal{D}_{v}, and then choose k\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}, again uniquely outside a null boundary set, such that x+\nu\cdot\widehat{\chi}-k\in\mathcal{D}_{h}.
Thus \mathcal{D}_{h}\times\mathcal{D}_{v} is a fundamental domain for \Gamma, up to its null boundary.
Let
\mathcal{H}\coloneqq(\mathcal{D}_{h}\times\mathcal{D}_{v})\setminus(\Gamma+K),\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal{H}_{w}\coloneqq\{x\in\mathcal{D}_{h}\colon(x,w)\in\mathcal{H}\}.
The set \Gamma+K is closed because K is compact and \Gamma is discrete.
Hence \mathcal{H} is Borel and its sections \mathcal{H}_{w} are measurable.
Fix w\in\mathcal{D}_{v}, and choose \lambda=B(\nu_{0}) and (P,\ell)\in\mathscr{A} from (4.12).
For \omega\in P, put \nu_{\omega}\coloneqq\nu_{0}+M\omega.
The points of \Gamma with vertical coordinate \lambda+\Psi(\omega)=B(\nu_{\omega}) are
\left(k-\nu_{\omega}\cdot\widehat{\chi},\,B(\nu_{\omega})\right),\quad\text{for }k\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}.
Suppose x\in\mathcal{H}_{w}.
If \pi(x+\nu_{\omega}\cdot\widehat{\chi}) belonged to \pi(J_{\ell(\omega)}), there would be a k\in\mathbb{Z}^{m} such that x-k+\nu_{\omega}\cdot\widehat{\chi}\in J_{\ell(\omega)}.
By (4.12), the difference between (x,w) and the corresponding point of \Gamma would then belong to K, contradicting x\in\mathcal{H}_{w}.
Therefore \pi(x+\nu_{\omega}\cdot\widehat{\chi})\in U_{\ell(\omega)} for every \omega\in P.
In \mathbb{T}^{m}, we have (M\omega)\cdot\chi=\omega\cdot(M^{\mathsf{T}}\chi)=\omega\cdot z.
It follows that the image of \mathcal{H}_{w} under the measure-preserving map x\mapsto\pi(x+\nu_{0}\cdot\widehat{\chi}) is contained in
\bigcap_{\omega\in P}\bigl(U_{\ell(\omega)}-\omega\cdot z\bigr).
The restriction of \pi to \mathcal{D}_{h} preserves measure up to the null boundary.
Hence Theorem 4.3 gives
\operatorname{vol}_{m}(\mathcal{H}_{w})\leq L^{|P|-1}\prod_{\omega\in P}\delta_{\ell(\omega)}.
The bound is uniform in w, even though the witness need not be chosen measurably.
Since \operatorname{vol}_{d}(\mathcal{D}_{v})=\det\Lambda_{v}, Tonelli’s theorem now gives
\bar{\rho}(\Gamma+K)=\frac{1}{\det\Lambda_{v}}\int_{\mathcal{D}_{v}}\operatorname{vol}_{m}(\mathcal{H}_{w})\,\,\mathrm{d}w\leq\max_{(P,\ell)\in\mathscr{A}}L^{|P|-1}\prod_{\omega\in P}\delta_{\ell(\omega)}.
Finally, define \Lambda\coloneqq(S^{-1}\oplus\operatorname{id}_{F})(\Gamma).
The inverse map preserves the uncovered proportion and gives \det\Lambda=\det\Lambda_{h}\det\Lambda_{v}.
This proves (4.13) and (4.14); taking logarithms proves (4.15).
∎
We finish with the form of entropy pruning used in the main proof.
It separates the vertical entropy estimates from the horizontal geometry.
A label map need not be injective: all sums and products indexed by Boolean vertices count repeated labels with their multiplicities.
Lemma 4.5.
Let m,d,N be positive integers, let \rho>0, and let u_{1},\ldots,u_{N}>0.
For \varepsilon\in\{0,1\}^{d}, let a_{\varepsilon}>0, and put A\coloneqq\sum_{\varepsilon}a_{\varepsilon} and q_{\varepsilon}\coloneqq a_{\varepsilon}/A.
Suppose that, for some \zeta\in[0,1/2], a label map \ell\colon\{0,1\}^{d}\to[N] satisfies
(1-\zeta)\rho a_{\varepsilon}\leq u_{\ell(\varepsilon)}\leq(1+\zeta)\rho a_{\varepsilon}.
(4.16)
For T_{0}>0, define the retained pattern P\coloneqq\{\varepsilon\colon\rho a_{\varepsilon}\geq 2T_{0}\}.
Then every retained label has load at least T_{0}.
If in addition
(1+\zeta)\rho A\max_{\varepsilon}q_{\varepsilon}\leq\eta_{m},
(4.17)
then every retained label has load at most \eta_{m}, and
\sum_{\varepsilon\in P}u_{\ell(\varepsilon)}\geq(1-\zeta)\rho A\left(1-\frac{H(q)}{\log(\rho A/(2T_{0}))}\right),
(4.18)
provided \rho A>2T_{0}.
Proof.
The lower and upper load bounds follow immediately from (4.16) and (4.17).
If \varepsilon\notin P, then q_{\varepsilon}<2T_{0}/(\rho A).
For every probability vector q and every \theta\in(0,1),
\sum_{q_{\varepsilon}\leq\theta}q_{\varepsilon}\leq\frac{H(q)}{\log(1/\theta)},
(4.19)
because each summand in the indicated set satisfies -q_{\varepsilon}\log q_{\varepsilon}\geq q_{\varepsilon}\log(1/\theta).
Apply (4.19) with \theta\coloneqq 2T_{0}/(\rho A), and use the lower bound in (4.16) on the retained vertices.
This proves (4.18).
∎
5 Proof of the universal upper bound
We prove the upper bound in four steps.
First, we normalize K, choose the vertical dimension, and discretize all relevant horizontal sections.
Second, the weighted full-cube construction supplies a vertical lattice and a Boolean family of Gaussian loads above every vertical translate.
Third, entropy pruning removes the small loads, after which the Rogers–Schmidt estimate gives one horizontal lattice for every surviving section label.
Finally, weighted lifting combines the horizontal and vertical lattices, and Rogers’ completion lemma turns the resulting almost covering into an exact covering.
Put \ell_{n}\coloneqq\log\log n.
For a sufficiently large absolute constant A, choose
d\coloneqq\left\lceil A\ell_{n}^{4/3}(\log\ell_{n})^{2/3}\right\rceil.
(5.1)
Set m\coloneqq n-d.
For orientation, the Gaussian width is \tau=(2\log d)^{-1}, the finite-field grid has size Q\asymp d(\log d)^{2}, and the vertical dimension satisfies d\asymp\ell_{n}^{4/3}(\log\ell_{n})^{2/3}.
Later, the number of section labels satisfies \log N_{0}=O(d\log n), the pruning threshold satisfies T_{0}=O(d\log n), and the target density is \rho=n\log n\,d^{5/2+o(1)}.
The first two parameters define the vertical cube and lattice; the choice of d provides the required min-entropy; N_{0} and T_{0} control the common-lattice union bound; and \rho provides the total horizontal load.
Unless explicitly stated otherwise, every o(1) term in this section is deterministic and uniform in the convex body K, the vertical translate w, and the Boolean vertex \varepsilon.
The next elementary estimates verify every range condition used below and show that the vertical factor d^{5/2+o(1)} becomes the stated power of \log\log n.
Lemma 5.1.
If A is sufficiently large, then
ds_{\infty}\geq 4\ell_{n},
(5.2)
and
d=o(n),\qquad d\log n=o(n),\qquad 4^{d}d\log n=o(n\log n),\qquad d\leq n^{c_{1}},\quad\text{and}\quad 2\sqrt{2}\,d^{3/2}\sqrt{\log d}=o(n^{c_{4}}).
Moreover,
d^{5/2+o(1)}=(\log\log n)^{10/3+o(1)}.
(5.3)
Proof.
The one-coordinate min-entropy estimate from Lemma 3.2 gives
ds_{\infty}=\left(\frac{2\pi-4}{\sqrt{\pi}}+o(1)\right)\frac{d^{3/4}}{\sqrt{\log d}}.
The choice (5.1) gives
\frac{d^{3/4}}{\sqrt{\log d}}=\left(\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}}\,A^{3/4}+o(1)\right)\ell_{n}.
Thus the last expression is (c_{A}+o(1))\ell_{n}, where c_{A}\coloneqq((2\pi-4)/\sqrt{\pi})\sqrt{3/4}\,A^{3/4}.
Since c_{A}\to\infty with A, taking A sufficiently large proves (5.2).
The remaining growth conditions follow because d is a fixed power of \log\log n, while \log n=\exp(\ell_{n}) and n=\exp(\exp(\ell_{n})).
In particular, 4^{d}d=\exp(O(d))=n^{o(1)}=o(n), which gives 4^{d}d\log n=o(n\log n).
Finally, raising (5.1) to the power 5/2 proves (5.3), with all lower-order factors absorbed into the o(1).
∎
Proof of Theorem 1.2.
Choose once and for all an absolute constant A large enough for Lemma 5.1, and then choose an absolute constant B_{0} with B_{0}\geq 8.
From this point on A and B_{0} are fixed in that order.
We take n\geq n_{0}(A,B_{0}), increasing n_{0}(A,B_{0}) whenever one of the uniform estimates below requires it.
We first choose a common affine normalization and vertical subspace.
Fix an arbitrary n-dimensional convex body.
By affine invariance, apply Proposition 4.1 with R\coloneqq\sqrt{d/\tau}=\sqrt{2d\log d}, and henceforth write K for the affine image given there.
Fix the resulting orthogonal decomposition \mathbb{R}^{n}=E\oplus F, identify F isometrically with \mathbb{R}^{d}, and retain the discretization bodies J_{1},\ldots,J_{N}.
Indeed,
2dR=2\sqrt{2}\,d^{3/2}\sqrt{\log d}<n^{c_{4}}
for all sufficiently large n by Lemma 5.1, so the range condition of the proposition holds.
Thus the vertical construction below is made in the same subspace F for which all the pointwise section comparisons and labels are available.
We now choose the target density and the corresponding vertical and horizontal determinants.
Apply the weighted vertical construction of Proposition 3.8.
Let \Lambda_{v}\subseteq F be its scaled vertical lattice, set \Psi\coloneqq\Psi_{d} and D_{v}\coloneqq\det\Lambda_{v}, and note that \Psi(\mathbb{Z}^{d})\subseteq\Lambda_{v} is a finite-index sublattice.
For a fixed w\in F, choose any \lambda_{w}\in\Lambda_{v} supplied by the construction and form the vertical points
y_{w,\varepsilon}\coloneqq w-\lambda_{w}-\Psi(\varepsilon),\quad\text{for }\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}^{d}.
All estimates below are uniform in w and hold for every admissible choice of \lambda_{w}; no choice as w varies will be required.
Using the notation of Proposition 3.8, set \mathsf{w}_{w,\varepsilon}\coloneqq D_{v}\gamma_{d}(y_{w,\varepsilon}), \mathsf{W}_{w}\coloneqq\sum_{\varepsilon}\mathsf{w}_{w,\varepsilon}, and q_{w,\varepsilon}\coloneqq\mathsf{w}_{w,\varepsilon}/\mathsf{W}_{w}, and write q_{w}\coloneqq(q_{w,\varepsilon})_{\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}^{d}}.
Let \xi_{d}=C_{\xi}\log\log d/\log d be the deterministic sequence in Proposition 3.8.
Since ds\asymp ds_{\infty}\asymp d^{3/4}/\sqrt{\log d}, for s_{\star}\in\{s,s_{\infty}\} we have
\frac{\sqrt{ds_{\star}\log d}+o(\log d)}{ds_{\star}}=O\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log d}{ds_{\star}}}\right)+o\left(\frac{\log d}{ds_{\star}}\right)=o\left(\frac{\log\log d}{\log d}\right).
After increasing the absolute constant C_{\xi} if necessary, the same sequence \xi_{d} therefore absorbs the error terms in both (3.44) and (3.45).
Thus, uniformly in w,
\displaystyle d^{-5/2-\xi_{d}}
\displaystyle\leq\mathsf{W}_{w}\leq d^{-5/2+\xi_{d}},
\displaystyle-\log\max_{\varepsilon}q_{w,\varepsilon}
\displaystyle\geq(1-\xi_{d})ds_{\infty},
\displaystyle H(q_{w})
\displaystyle\leq(1+\xi_{d})ds.
(5.4)
Set the target density to be
\rho\coloneqq B_{0}n\log n\,d^{5/2+\xi_{d}}.
(5.5)
Choose the horizontal determinant D_{h}\coloneqq\operatorname{vol}_{n}(K)/(\rho D_{v}).
The ideal horizontal load of the point y_{w,\varepsilon} is \widehat{u}_{w,\varepsilon}\coloneqq\rho\mathsf{w}_{w,\varepsilon}.
By (5.4),
\sum_{\varepsilon}\widehat{u}_{w,\varepsilon}=\rho\mathsf{W}_{w}\geq B_{0}n\log n.
(5.6)
On the other hand, (5.2) and (5.4), together with the initial choice of A, imply
\max_{\varepsilon}\widehat{u}_{w,\varepsilon}\leq B_{0}n\log n\,d^{2\xi_{d}}e^{-(1-\xi_{d})ds_{\infty}}\leq B_{0}n\log n\,e^{-(1-2\xi_{d})ds_{\infty}}\leq\frac{1}{4}\eta_{m}
(5.7)
for all n\geq n_{0}(A,B_{0}); in the second inequality we used 2\log d\leq ds_{\infty}, which holds for large d.
Indeed, (5.2) and \xi_{d}\to 0 make the preceding quantity at most
B_{0}n(\log n)^{-3+8\xi_{d}},
which is o(n), whereas \eta_{m}=b_{0}(n-d)-3\log(n-d)\sim b_{0}n.
We next prune the small loads and assign the corresponding section labels.
Fix an absolute constant C_{\mathrm{sec}} at least as large as the constant in Proposition 4.1 and such that C_{\mathrm{sec}}\geq 2(1+c_{\mathrm{RS}}).
Let N_{0}\coloneqq(C_{\mathrm{sec}}m^{2})^{d} be the deterministic upper bound in the section discretization, and put T_{0}\coloneqq 4\log(C_{\mathrm{sec}}N_{0}).
Since T_{0}=O(d\log n)=o(n\log n), (5.6) implies \rho\mathsf{W}_{w}>2T_{0}, uniformly in w, for all sufficiently large n.
All the points y_{w,\varepsilon} lie in B_{R}^{d}.
Put u_{a}\coloneqq\operatorname{vol}_{m}(J_{a})/D_{h}.
For a fixed admissible vertical witness and every \varepsilon\in\{0,1\}^{d}, choose any label \alpha_{w}(\varepsilon)\in[N] furnished by Proposition 4.1, so that (4.3) and (4.4) hold for this same label.
By (4.5) and the definition of D_{h}, the normalization is
\displaystyle u_{\alpha_{w}(\varepsilon)}=\frac{\operatorname{vol}_{m}(J_{\alpha_{w}(\varepsilon)})}{D_{h}}
\displaystyle=\left(1+O\left(\frac{1}{m}+n^{-c_{3}}\right)\right)\frac{\operatorname{vol}_{n}(K)\gamma_{d}(y_{w,\varepsilon})}{\operatorname{vol}_{n}(K)/(\rho D_{v})}
\displaystyle=\left(1+O\left(\frac{1}{m}+n^{-c_{3}}\right)\right)\rho D_{v}\gamma_{d}(y_{w,\varepsilon})
\displaystyle=\left(1+O\left(\frac{1}{m}+n^{-c_{3}}\right)\right)\rho\mathsf{w}_{w,\varepsilon}=\left(1+O\left(\frac{1}{m}+n^{-c_{3}}\right)\right)\widehat{u}_{w,\varepsilon}.
In particular, there is a deterministic sequence \zeta_{n}\to 0, independent of K,w,\varepsilon, such that 0\leq\zeta_{n}\leq 1/2 and
(1-\zeta_{n})\widehat{u}_{w,\varepsilon}\leq u_{\alpha_{w}(\varepsilon)}\leq(1+\zeta_{n})\widehat{u}_{w,\varepsilon}.
For each w, define the retained pattern
\mathcal{P}_{w}\coloneqq\{\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}^{d}\colon\widehat{u}_{w,\varepsilon}\geq 2T_{0}\}.
Equations (5.6) and (5.7) imply
