(1+\zeta_{n})\rho\mathsf{W}_{w}\max_{\varepsilon}q_{w,\varepsilon}\leq\eta_{m}
for n\geq n_{0}(A,B_{0}).
Apply Lemma 4.5 for each w with
a_{\varepsilon}=\mathsf{w}_{w,\varepsilon},\qquad A=\mathsf{W}_{w},\qquad q=q_{w},\qquad\ell=\alpha_{w},\quad\text{and}\quad\zeta=\zeta_{n}.
Every label occurring in \mathcal{P}_{w} then lies in the common load window
T_{0}\leq u_{a}\leq\eta_{m}.
(5.8)
By Lemma 3.2 and (5.1), there is an absolute constant c>0 such that, uniformly in w,
\displaystyle H(q_{w})\leq(1+\xi_{d})ds=O(\ell_{n})\quad\text{and}\quad\log\frac{\rho\mathsf{W}_{w}}{2T_{0}}\geq\log\frac{cn}{d}=\log n-O(\log d)=(1-o(1))\log n.
Thus H(q_{w})/\log(\rho\mathsf{W}_{w}/(2T_{0}))=O(\ell_{n}/\log n)=o(1).
The retained-load conclusion of Lemma 4.5 therefore yields
\sum_{\varepsilon\in\mathcal{P}_{w}}u_{\alpha_{w}(\varepsilon)}\geq(1-o(1))B_{0}n\log n
(5.9)
uniformly in w.
It remains to choose one horizontal lattice and complete the covering.
Let \mathscr{A}_{0} be the set of all labeled retained patterns that can arise from the preceding construction: choose w\in F, an admissible vertical witness \lambda_{w}, and labels satisfying the section inclusions, and retain the resulting pair (\mathcal{P}_{w},\alpha_{w}|_{\mathcal{P}_{w}}).
This is an existential definition and makes no global choice as w varies.
The family \mathscr{A}_{0} is finite because \mathcal{P}_{w} is a subset of the finite Boolean cube and its labels lie in [N].
By (5.9), every pattern in \mathscr{A}_{0} is nonempty for sufficiently large n, and the retained-load bound holds uniformly over the family.
Call a label active if it appears in a member of \mathscr{A}_{0}, and let \mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{act}} be the set of active labels.
It is finite; set N_{\mathrm{act}}\coloneqq|\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{act}}|\leq N_{0}.
Discard the unused discretization bodies and reindex the bodies in \mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{act}}, together with every map in \mathscr{A}_{0}, by [N_{\mathrm{act}}].
Denote the resulting family of labeled patterns by \mathscr{A}.
Thus (5.8) holds for every label in this reindexed family.
Apply Lemma 4.2 to this reindexed family, with determinant D_{h}.
We have
T_{0}=4\log(C_{\mathrm{sec}}N_{0})\geq 2\log\bigl(2(1+c_{\mathrm{RS}})N_{\mathrm{act}}\bigr).
Together with (5.8), these are the hypotheses of that lemma.
We obtain one horizontal lattice \Lambda_{h} such that every active label satisfies
\bar{\rho}(\Lambda_{h}+J_{a})\leq e^{-u_{a}/2}.
(5.10)
Put \mathscr{C}\coloneqq\operatorname{scl}(\mathscr{A}) and L\coloneqq 2|\mathscr{C}|.
For every w, the vertical construction and the section discretization supply at least one member (P,\alpha)\in\mathscr{A} and a \lambda\in\Lambda_{v} satisfying the witness condition (4.12).
Thus the lifting theorem requires no measurable selection.
Moreover, \mathscr{C} is contained in the family of all labeled subpatterns of the Boolean cube, and hence
\log L\leq C2^{d}\log(N_{0}+1).
For every (P,\alpha)\in\mathscr{A}, one has |P|-1\leq 2^{d}.
Since \log(N_{0}+1)=O(d\log n), Lemma 5.1 therefore gives
(|P|-1)\log L\leq C4^{d}\log(N_{0}+1)=O(4^{d}d\log n)=o(n\log n).
Apply Theorem 4.4 with \delta_{a}=e^{-u_{a}/2} and c=1/2.
Together with (5.10) and (5.9), it produces a lattice \Lambda\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} with \det\Lambda=D_{h}D_{v} and
\displaystyle\log\bar{\rho}(\Lambda+K)\leq C4^{d}\log(N_{0}+1)-\frac{1}{2}\min_{(P,\alpha)\in\mathscr{A}}\sum_{\varepsilon\in P}u_{\alpha(\varepsilon)}\leq\left(-\frac{1}{2}(1-o(1))B_{0}+o(1)\right)n\log n.
Because B_{0}\geq 8 was fixed before n_{0}(A,B_{0}), the last expression is smaller than -2n\log n after one final increase of n_{0}(A,B_{0}).
Since e^{-2n\log n}=n^{-2n}<(n^{n}+1)^{-1}, it follows that
\bar{\rho}(\Lambda+K)<(n^{n}+1)^{-1}.
By Lemma 2.2, \Lambda+(1+1/n)K=\mathbb{R}^{n}.
Equivalently, \Lambda^{\prime}\coloneqq(1+1/n)^{-1}\Lambda satisfies \Lambda^{\prime}+K=\mathbb{R}^{n}.
Since \det\Lambda^{\prime}=(1+1/n)^{-n}\det\Lambda, the density of this exact lattice covering is
\frac{\operatorname{vol}_{n}(K)}{\det\Lambda^{\prime}}=\left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right)^{n}\frac{\operatorname{vol}_{n}(K)}{D_{h}D_{v}}\leq e\rho.
It remains to express the auxiliary dimension in the form used in the theorem.
Since \log d=(4/3)\log\ell_{n}+(2/3)\log\log\ell_{n}+O(1), we have
\frac{(5/2+\xi_{d})\log d}{\log\ell_{n}}=\frac{10}{3}+\frac{4}{3}\xi_{d}+\left(\frac{5}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\xi_{d}\right)\frac{\log\log\ell_{n}}{\log\ell_{n}}+O\left(\frac{1}{\log\ell_{n}}\right).
For all sufficiently large n, define
\varepsilon_{n}\coloneqq\max\left\{0,\,\frac{(5/2+\xi_{d})\log d}{\log\ell_{n}}-\frac{10}{3}\right\}.
Set \varepsilon_{n}\coloneqq 0 for the remaining finitely many n.
Then \varepsilon_{n}\to 0, independently of K, and d^{5/2+\xi_{d}}\leq\ell_{n}^{10/3+\varepsilon_{n}} for all sufficiently large n.
Consequently, (5.5) gives
\theta_{L}(K)\leq eB_{0}n\log n\,(\log\log n)^{10/3+\varepsilon_{n}}.
Finally, affine invariance permits us to undo the normalization without changing the covering density.
The constants and the sequence \varepsilon_{n} are independent of K, so taking the supremum over all n-dimensional convex bodies proves Theorem 1.2 with C=eB_{0}.
∎
Part II Worst-case lower bounds
The lower-bound argument is technically independent of Part I.
We therefore introduce its spherical, Poisson, and flat-torus notation locally.
6 Tools for the lower bound
The proof uses three auxiliary tools.
Spherical-cap estimates control intersections among the sets of Poisson directions that cut prescribed residual vectors.
A packing argument on a flat torus produces many targets with separated residual directions.
Finally, a continuous Janson inequality converts bounds for the resulting Poisson witnesses and their dependency diagrams into a small covering probability for a fixed lattice.
We write B_{2}^{n} for the Euclidean unit ball, \mathbb{S}^{n-1} for its boundary, \kappa_{n}\coloneqq\operatorname{vol}_{n}(B_{2}^{n}), and \sigma for the rotation-invariant probability measure on \mathbb{S}^{n-1}.
Throughout Part II, the symbols c and C denote positive absolute constants whose values may change from one occurrence to the next.
Every other constant is fixed within the statement or proof in which it is introduced, and the constants in the hierarchy of Section 9 remain fixed thereafter.
Any dependence on fixed parameters is stated explicitly.
For r>1, let
p_{n}(r)\coloneqq\sigma\{u\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\colon|u_{1}|>1/r\}.
For nonzero vectors x and z in \mathbb{R}^{n}, define their projective angle by
\angle_{\mathrm{proj}}(x,z)\coloneqq\min\{\angle(x,z),\pi-\angle(x,z)\}.
6.1 Spherical caps
The following estimates will be used repeatedly.
The uniformity over a shell of width O(\log n/n) is essential later.
Lemma 6.1.
Fix a>1 and positive constants A and \beta, and put L\coloneqq a^{2}-1.
The following assertions hold for all sufficiently large n, where the lower threshold for n may depend on the fixed parameters displayed in the relevant assertion.
(i)
There is a constant C_{\mathrm{rad}}=C_{\mathrm{rad}}(a,A,\beta)>0 such that, if |t|\leq A\log n+\beta and r=ae^{t/n}, then
C_{\mathrm{rad}}^{-1}e^{t/L}\leq\frac{p_{n}(r)}{p_{n}(a)}\leq C_{\mathrm{rad}}e^{t/L}.
(ii)
For every compact interval I\subseteq(0,1) and every H_{0}>0, there is a constant H_{1}=H_{1}(I,H_{0})>0 such that, for every \tau\in I and 0\leq h\leq H_{0}\log n/n,
\frac{\sigma\{u\colon u_{1}>\tau+h\}}{\sigma\{u\colon u_{1}>\tau\}}\geq\exp(-H_{1}nh-H_{1}).
(iii)
Let r_{0}\coloneqq ae^{-A\log n/n} and b\coloneqq ae^{\beta/n}. For
r,s\in[r_{0}-n^{-4},b+n^{-4}], define
C(x)\coloneqq\{u\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\colon|\langle u,x\rangle|>1\}.
For every fixed J>0, there is a constant D=D(a,A,\beta,J)>0 such that, whenever |x|=r, |z|=s, and \angle_{\mathrm{proj}}(x,z)\geq D\sqrt{(\log n)/n}, we have
\sigma(C(x)\cap C(z))\leq n^{-J}\min\{\sigma(C(x)),\sigma(C(z))\}.
The same conclusion holds when the threshold 1 in both caps is replaced by 1+\eta, uniformly for 0\leq\eta\leq n^{-4}.
Proof.
The first coordinate of a uniform point of \mathbb{S}^{n-1} has density
f_{n}(s)\coloneqq c_{n}(1-s^{2})^{(n-3)/2},\quad\text{where}\quad c_{n}\coloneqq\frac{\Gamma(n/2)}{\sqrt{\pi}\,\Gamma((n-1)/2)}\asymp\sqrt{n}.
If \tau lies in a fixed compact subinterval of (0,1), then
\int_{\tau}^{1}f_{n}(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\asymp n^{-1/2}(1-\tau^{2})^{(n-1)/2}.
(6.1)
Indeed,
\int_{\tau}^{1}s(1-s^{2})^{(n-3)/2}\,\mathrm{d}s=\frac{(1-\tau^{2})^{(n-1)/2}}{n-1}.
On the interval of integration, the factor s lies between \tau and 1.
Removing this factor changes the integral by a bounded factor, and c_{n}\asymp\sqrt{n} gives (6.1).
For part (i), apply (6.1) with \tau=1/r.
When r=ae^{t/n}, Taylor expansion gives
\frac{n-1}{2}\bigl[\log(1-r^{-2})-\log(1-a^{-2})\bigr]=\frac{t}{a^{2}-1}+O\left(\frac{t^{2}+|t|}{n}\right).
The error is o(1) uniformly for |t|\leq A\log n+\beta, and the remaining factors in (6.1) have bounded ratios.
This proves part (i).
For part (ii), put p(\zeta)\coloneqq\int_{\zeta}^{1}f_{n}(s)\,\mathrm{d}s.
The endpoint estimate implies
-\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\zeta}\log p(\zeta)\leq Cn
uniformly on the fixed threshold interval.
Integrating from \tau to \tau+h yields
\log\frac{p(\tau+h)}{p(\tau)}\geq-Cnh.
For sufficiently large n, the point \tau+h remains in a slightly larger compact subinterval of (0,1).
Part (ii) follows after adjusting the constant.
It remains to prove part (iii).
Split each absolute cap into two oriented caps.
The shell assumptions place all oriented thresholds in a fixed compact interval [\tau_{0},\tau_{1}]\subsetneq(0,1) and give
|\tau-\xi|\leq C_{2}\frac{\log n}{n}.
(6.2)
Let e and f be unit vectors with angle \psi, and define
q_{*}(\tau,\xi,\psi)\coloneqq\min\{|v|^{2}\colon\langle v,e\rangle\geq\tau\text{ and }\langle v,f\rangle\geq\xi\}.
We first show that there are constants c_{3},C_{3}>0 such that
\psi^{2}\geq C_{3}\frac{\log n}{n}
(6.3)
implies
q_{*}(\tau,\xi,\psi)\geq\max\{\tau^{2},\xi^{2}\}+c_{3}\psi^{2},
(6.4)
unless the two constraints have empty intersection with the unit ball.
Fix a small constant \psi_{0}>0.
Suppose first that 0<\psi\leq\psi_{0} and, by symmetry, that \tau\geq\xi.
In coordinates e=(1,0) and f=(\cos\psi,\sin\psi), we have
\xi-\tau\cos\psi=\tau(1-\cos\psi)-(\tau-\xi).
By (6.2) and (6.3), a sufficiently large choice of C_{3} makes the right side at least c\psi^{2}.
Both constraints are therefore active at the minimizer, and
q_{*}(\tau,\xi,\psi)=\tau^{2}+\frac{(\xi-\tau\cos\psi)^{2}}{\sin^{2}\psi}\geq\tau^{2}+c\psi^{2}.
The case \xi\geq\tau is symmetric.
Now suppose that \psi\geq\psi_{0}.
If the oriented caps intersect the unit ball, then
\tau+\xi\leq|e+f|=2\cos(\psi/2),
and hence \psi\leq\pi-\delta_{0} for some fixed \delta_{0}>0.
At equal thresholds, the minimum norm exceeds the square of the threshold by a positive amount uniformly for \psi\in[\psi_{0},\pi-\delta_{0}].
Continuity gives the same conclusion when |\tau-\xi| is sufficiently small, and (6.2) supplies this smallness for large n.
After decreasing c_{3}, we again obtain (6.4).
Let P denote orthogonal projection onto \operatorname{span}\{e,f\}.
If u is uniform on \mathbb{S}^{n-1}, then
\mathbb{P}\left[|Pu|^{2}\geq q\right]=(1-q)^{(n-2)/2}\quad\text{for}\quad 0\leq q\leq 1.
Together with (6.1) and (6.4), this gives
\frac{\sigma\{u\colon\langle u,e\rangle>\tau\text{ and }\langle u,f\rangle>\xi\}}{\min\{\sigma\{u\colon\langle u,e\rangle>\tau\},\sigma\{u\colon\langle u,f\rangle>\xi\}\}}\leq n^{C_{4}}e^{-c_{4}n\psi^{2}}.
(6.5)
Indeed, the numerator is at most (1-q_{*})^{(n-2)/2}, while the smaller one-cap probability has threshold \max\{\tau,\xi\} and is bounded below by (6.1).
For two absolute caps, two sign choices have angle equal to the projective angle, and the other two have angle at least \pi/2.
Apply (6.5) to all four pairs.
Taking D sufficiently large gives the factor n^{-J}.
Replacing the threshold 1 by 1+\eta changes each oriented threshold by O(n^{-4}), so the preceding estimates remain uniform for 0\leq\eta\leq n^{-4}.
∎
6.2 Unfolding on a flat torus
For a lattice \Lambda, let \mathbb{T}_{\Lambda}\coloneqq\mathbb{R}^{n}/\Lambda, equipped with normalized Haar measure.
If y\in\mathbb{T}_{\Lambda}, an expression involving the coset y-\Lambda is evaluated using any representative of y; the result is independent of that choice.
In particular, for every nonnegative measurable function f, the sum below is a well-defined function on \mathbb{T}_{\Lambda}, and we use the unfolding identity
\int_{\mathbb{T}_{\Lambda}}\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}f(y-\lambda)\,\mathrm{d}y=\frac{1}{\det\Lambda}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x.
(6.6)
To obtain this identity, integrate over a fundamental domain and translate its lattice copies.
The next packing lemma does not require the quotient map to be injective on a small Euclidean ball.
Lemma 6.2.
Let G\subseteq\mathbb{T}_{\Lambda} have Haar measure at least \gamma>0, and let \delta>0.
There are points y_{1},\ldots,y_{T}\in G such that \operatorname{dist}_{\mathbb{T}_{\Lambda}}(y_{\alpha}-y_{\beta},0)>\delta and \operatorname{dist}_{\mathbb{T}_{\Lambda}}(y_{\alpha}+y_{\beta},0)>\delta for all distinct \alpha and \beta, and such that T\geq\gamma\det\Lambda/(2\kappa_{n}\delta^{n}).
Proof.
Choose the points greedily.
After selecting a point y, remove from G the images of the two closed balls y+\delta B_{2}^{n} and -y+\delta B_{2}^{n}.
The selected points satisfy both separation conditions.
Since every \delta-separated subset of the compact torus is finite, the process ends with a maximal list y_{1},\ldots,y_{T}.
The image of a Euclidean ball of radius \delta has normalized Haar measure at most \kappa_{n}\delta^{n}/\det\Lambda; identifications under the quotient map can only decrease its measure.
By maximality, the 2T removed images cover G.
Hence
\gamma\leq\frac{2T\kappa_{n}\delta^{n}}{\det\Lambda},
which proves the lemma.
∎
6.3 A continuous Janson inequality
Here a witness is an injective tuple of Poisson points chosen from prescribed measurable slots.
The diagram sums below record the ways in which two witnesses can share Poisson points.
Let (\Omega,\mu) be a finite nonatomic standard Borel measure space, and let \Pi be a Poisson process with intensity measure \mu.
Let \mathcal{A} be a finite index set.
For each \alpha\in\mathcal{A}, let I_{\alpha} be a finite nonempty set.
For every i\in I_{\alpha}, let E_{\alpha i}\subseteq\Omega be measurable with 0<\mu(E_{\alpha i})<\infty, and put
\lambda_{\alpha i}\coloneqq\mu(E_{\alpha i})\quad\text{and}\quad\nu_{\alpha}\coloneqq\prod_{i\in I_{\alpha}}\lambda_{\alpha i}.
Let Z_{\alpha} count the injective tuples (u_{i})_{i\in I_{\alpha}} of points of \Pi such that u_{i}\in E_{\alpha i} for every i\in I_{\alpha}.
The Campbell–Mecke formula [22] gives
\mathbb{E}Z_{\alpha}=\int_{\Omega_{\neq}^{I_{\alpha}}}\prod_{i\in I_{\alpha}}\mathbf{1}_{E_{\alpha i}}(u_{i})\,\,\mathrm{d}\mu^{\otimes I_{\alpha}}((u_{i})_{i})=\prod_{i\in I_{\alpha}}\lambda_{\alpha i}=\nu_{\alpha},
where \Omega_{\neq}^{I_{\alpha}} is the set of tuples with pairwise distinct coordinates.
Its complement has product measure zero because \mu is nonatomic.
Thus \nu_{\alpha} is the mean number of witnesses of type \alpha.
A partial injection M\colon I_{\alpha}\dashrightarrow I_{\beta} is an injective map from a subset of I_{\alpha} into I_{\beta}.
For a nonempty partial injection M, define
W_{\alpha\beta}(M)\coloneqq\nu_{\alpha}\nu_{\beta}\prod_{(i,j)\in M}\frac{\mu(E_{\alpha i}\cap E_{\beta j})}{\lambda_{\alpha i}\lambda_{\beta j}}.
(6.7)
Let D_{\alpha\beta} be the sum of (6.7) over all nonempty partial injections from I_{\alpha} to I_{\beta}.
We first record the finite indexed form of Janson’s inequality that will be used in the approximation.
Lemma 6.3.
Let (X_{v})_{v\in V} be independent Bernoulli variables on a finite set V, and let (H_{h})_{h\in\mathcal{H}} be a finite indexed family of nonempty subsets of V.
Repetitions among the underlying subsets are allowed.
Put
I_{h}\coloneqq\prod_{v\in H_{h}}X_{v},\qquad Y\coloneqq\sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}}I_{h},\quad\text{and}\quad m\coloneqq\mathbb{E}Y,
and define the ordered dependency sum, including the diagonal, by
\Delta^{*}\coloneqq\sum_{(h,h^{\prime})\colon H_{h}\cap H_{h^{\prime}}\neq\varnothing}\mathbb{E}(I_{h}I_{h^{\prime}}).
If m>0, then
\mathbb{P}\left[Y=0\right]\leq\exp\left(-\frac{m^{2}}{2\Delta^{*}}\right).
(6.8)
Proof.
For distinct underlying subsets, (6.8) is the lower-tail form of Janson’s inequality with t=m; see Janson, Łuczak, and Ruciński [17, Theorem 2.14].
With our ordered convention, \Delta^{*} is the quantity denoted there by \bar{\Delta}.
To remove the distinctness assumption, fix 0<\varepsilon<1.
For each index h, introduce a private Bernoulli variable B_{h} with parameter 1-\varepsilon.
Assume that all private variables are independent of one another and of the original family, and replace I_{h} by I_{h}B_{h}.
The augmented underlying sets are distinct.
Their mean and ordered dependency sum are
m_{\varepsilon}=(1-\varepsilon)m
and
\Delta_{\varepsilon}^{*}=(1-\varepsilon)\sum_{h}\mathbb{E}I_{h}+(1-\varepsilon)^{2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}h\neq h^{\prime}\\
H_{h}\cap H_{h^{\prime}}\neq\varnothing\end{subarray}}\mathbb{E}(I_{h}I_{h^{\prime}}).
The probability that the augmented family has no present member differs from \mathbb{P}\left[Y=0\right] by at most |\mathcal{H}|\varepsilon.
Since m_{\varepsilon}\to m and \Delta_{\varepsilon}^{*}\to\Delta^{*}, letting \varepsilon\downarrow 0 proves the indexed form.
∎
Lemma 6.4.
There is an absolute constant c>0 such that
\mathbb{P}\left[Z_{\alpha}=0\text{ for every }\alpha\right]\leq\exp\left(-c\frac{(\sum_{\alpha}\nu_{\alpha})^{2}}{\sum_{\alpha,\beta}D_{\alpha\beta}}\right).
(6.9)
In particular, D_{\alpha\alpha} contains the full diagonal matching, whose weight is \nu_{\alpha}.
Proof.
We approximate the Poisson process by independent cell-occupancy variables.
All sets may first be modified on null sets, so we may assume that they are Borel.
Nested partitions.
The standard Borel structure has a countable family of Borel sets that separates points.
Start with the Boolean atoms generated by the finitely many sets E_{\alpha i}.
At stage k, refine the preceding partition by the first k point-separating Borel sets.
Using nonatomicity, subdivide every positive-measure cell into finitely many measurable pieces of measure at most 2^{-k}.
These choices can be made recursively, so they give nested finite partitions (\mathcal{P}_{k})_{k\geq 1}.
After discarding null cells, we have
\delta_{k}\coloneqq\max_{C\in\mathcal{P}_{k}}\mu(C)\longrightarrow 0.
Every cell is contained in or disjoint from each E_{\alpha i}, and every two distinct points of \Omega are eventually separated by the partitions.
For C\in\mathcal{P}_{k}, let X_{C} indicate that \Pi meets C.
The variables (X_{C})_{C\in\mathcal{P}_{k}} are independent, and
q_{C}\coloneqq\mathbb{P}\left[X_{C}=1\right]=1-e^{-\mu(C)}=\mu(C)(1+O(\delta_{k}))
(6.10)
uniformly in C.
An indexed hyperedge consists of a label \alpha and an assignment (C_{i})_{i\in I_{\alpha}} of pairwise distinct cells satisfying C_{i}\subseteq E_{\alpha i} for every i.
Its underlying vertex set is \{C_{i}\colon i\in I_{\alpha}\}, and its indicator is \prod_{i}X_{C_{i}}.
Different labels and different assignments remain distinct indices even when they have the same underlying cell set.
Let Y_{k} count the present indexed hyperedges, let m_{k}\coloneqq\mathbb{E}Y_{k}, and let \Delta_{k}^{*} be the ordered dependency sum from Lemma 6.3.
Then
\mathbb{P}\left[Y_{k}=0\right]\leq\exp\left(-\frac{m_{k}^{2}}{2\Delta_{k}^{*}}\right)
(6.11)
whenever m_{k}>0.
First moment.
Fix \alpha and put s_{\alpha}\coloneqq|I_{\alpha}|.
By (6.10),
\mathbb{E}Y_{k,\alpha}=\bigl(1+O(s_{\alpha}\delta_{k})\bigr)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(C_{i})_{i\in I_{\alpha}}\text{ pairwise distinct}\\
C_{i}\subseteq E_{\alpha i}\end{subarray}}\prod_{i\in I_{\alpha}}\mu(C_{i}).
(6.12)
Without the distinctness restriction, the sum equals \nu_{\alpha}.
For fixed distinct i and j, assignments with C_{i}=C_{j} have total product mass at most
\sum_{C\subseteq E_{\alpha i}\cap E_{\alpha j}}\mu(C)^{2}\prod_{\ell\neq i,j}\lambda_{\alpha\ell}\leq\delta_{k}\mu(E_{\alpha i}\cap E_{\alpha j})\prod_{\ell\neq i,j}\lambda_{\alpha\ell}.
A union bound over the finitely many pairs of slots shows that
m_{k}\longrightarrow\sum_{\alpha}\nu_{\alpha}.
(6.13)
In particular, m_{k}>0 for all sufficiently large k.
Dependency sum.
Fix \alpha, \beta, and a nonempty partial injection M\colon I_{\alpha}\dashrightarrow I_{\beta}.
Form the quotient of the disjoint union I_{\alpha}\sqcup I_{\beta} by identifying i and j whenever (i,j)\in M.
For each quotient class Q, let F_{Q} be the intersection of the one or two slot sets indexed by Q.
If the quotient classes choose cells independently and unintended equalities are ignored, their total product mass is
\prod_{Q}\mu(F_{Q})=\nu_{\alpha}\nu_{\beta}\prod_{(i,j)\in M}\frac{\mu(E_{\alpha i}\cap E_{\beta j})}{\lambda_{\alpha i}\lambda_{\beta j}}=W_{\alpha\beta}(M).
If two distinct quotient classes Q and Q^{\prime} use the same cell, then the total product mass is at most
\delta_{k}\mu(F_{Q}\cap F_{Q^{\prime}})\prod_{Q^{\prime\prime}\neq Q,Q^{\prime}}\mu(F_{Q^{\prime\prime}}).
There are finitely many pairs of quotient classes, so requiring the quotient classes to use pairwise distinct cells changes the total by O(\delta_{k}).
For two internally injective cell assignments, the complete set of cross equalities is uniquely a partial injection: each cell on the left equals at most one cell on the right, and conversely.
The two indexed hyperedges intersect exactly when this partial injection is nonempty.
Hence the ordered dependency sum decomposes without omission or repetition over the nonempty partial injections.
Replacing each factor \mu(C) by q_{C} changes each finite sum by another O(\delta_{k}), by (6.10).
Therefore
\Delta_{k}^{*}\longrightarrow\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{A}}D_{\alpha\beta}.
(6.14)
Limiting event.
Because the partitions are nested, the events \{Y_{k}>0\} increase with k.
A witness in pairwise distinct coarse cells remains a witness after one occupied subcell is chosen inside each coarse cell.
Conversely, the Poisson process is finite and simple almost surely because \mu(\Omega)<\infty and \mu is nonatomic.
Every finite list of distinct Poisson points is eventually separated by the partitions.
Consequently,
\bigcup_{k}\{Y_{k}>0\}=\left\{\sum_{\alpha}Z_{\alpha}>0\right\}\quad\text{almost surely}.
Thus
\mathbb{P}\left[Y_{k}=0\right]\downarrow\mathbb{P}\left[Z_{\alpha}=0\text{ for every }\alpha\right].
Letting k\to\infty in (6.11), and using (6.13) and (6.14), proves (6.9) with c=1/2.
For \alpha=\beta, the full matching i\mapsto i has weight \nu_{\alpha}^{2}\prod_{i}\lambda_{\alpha i}^{-1}=\nu_{\alpha}.
∎
For distinct \alpha and \beta, put
\rho_{\alpha\beta}\coloneqq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\in I_{\alpha}\\
j\in I_{\beta}\end{subarray}}\frac{\mu(E_{\alpha i}\cap E_{\beta j})}{\lambda_{\alpha i}\lambda_{\beta j}}.
(6.15)
Dropping the matching constraint and expanding the resulting product gives
D_{\alpha\beta}\leq\nu_{\alpha}\nu_{\beta}\bigl(e^{\rho_{\alpha\beta}}-1\bigr).
(6.16)
This estimate is the interface used later to convert cross-target cap overlaps into the dependency term in the continuous Janson inequality.
7 The random convex body
The construction has three components.
The cube fixes the John normalization, the outer Euclidean ball gives a uniform radius bound, and the random slabs create many potential holes while preserving a constant fraction of the volume with positive probability.
For the remainder of the lower-bound argument, fix
a\coloneqq 2,\qquad L\coloneqq a^{2}-1=3,\quad\text{and}\quad\beta\coloneqq 1,
and put b\coloneqq ae^{\beta/n}.
Let \Pi be a Poisson process on \mathbb{S}^{n-1} with intensity measure
\mu\coloneqq M\sigma,\quad\text{where}\quad M\coloneqq\frac{L}{p_{n}(a)}.
This normalization gives Mp_{n}(a)=L, so the cap associated with a residual vector of norm a has constant intensity.
It balances the random cuts against survival of a constant fraction of the volume.
Define
K_{\Pi}\coloneqq bB_{2}^{n}\cap[-1,1]^{n}\cap\bigcap_{u\in\Pi}\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\colon|\langle u,x\rangle|\leq 1\}.
(7.1)
The set K_{\Pi} is an origin-symmetric convex body, and
B_{2}^{n}\subseteq K_{\Pi}\subseteq[-1,1]^{n}\cap bB_{2}^{n}.
Proposition 7.1.
There are absolute constants c_{v},c_{p}>0 such that, for all sufficiently large n,
\mathbb{P}\left[\operatorname{vol}_{n}(K_{\Pi})\geq c_{v}\kappa_{n}a^{n}\right]\geq c_{p}.
For every realization of \Pi, the John ellipsoid of K_{\Pi} is B_{2}^{n}.
Proof.
For a vector x with |x|=r>1, let
C_{x}\coloneqq\{u\colon|\langle u,x\rangle|>1\}\quad\text{and}\quad c(x)\coloneqq\mu(C_{x})=Mp_{n}(r).
The Poisson void probability gives
\mathbb{P}\left[\Pi\cap C_{x}=\varnothing\right]=e^{-c(x)}.
Restrict polar integration to the shell r\in[ae^{-1/n},a].
By Lemma 6.1(i), the quantity c(x) is bounded above by an absolute constant throughout this shell.
If v is uniform on \mathbb{S}^{n-1}, then, for every such r,
\mathbb{P}\left[rv\notin[-1,1]^{n}\right]\leq n\mathbb{P}\left[|v_{1}|>1/a\right]\leq ne^{-cn}=o(1),
where the last inequality follows from (6.1).
Fubini’s theorem therefore gives
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\operatorname{vol}_{n}(K_{\Pi})
\displaystyle\geq(1-o(1))e^{-C}\operatorname{vol}_{n}\bigl(aB_{2}^{n}\setminus ae^{-1/n}B_{2}^{n}\bigr)
\displaystyle\geq c\kappa_{n}a^{n}.
We also have \operatorname{vol}_{n}(K_{\Pi})\leq\kappa_{n}b^{n}=e^{\beta}\kappa_{n}a^{n}.
Let X\coloneqq\operatorname{vol}_{n}(K_{\Pi}) and t\coloneqq(c/2)\kappa_{n}a^{n}.
Since
X\leq t+e^{\beta}\kappa_{n}a^{n}\mathbf{1}_{\{X\geq t\}},
the expectation bound implies
\mathbb{P}\left[X\geq\frac{c}{2}\kappa_{n}a^{n}\right]\geq\frac{c}{2e^{\beta}}.
This proves the first assertion after renaming the constants.
It remains to identify the John ellipsoid.
The contact points \pm e_{i} of the cube, each with weight 1/2, satisfy
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}}\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon e_{i}=0\quad\text{and}\quad\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}}\frac{1}{2}(\varepsilon e_{i})(\varepsilon e_{i})^{\mathsf{T}}=I_{n}.
By John’s contact criterion [19, 1], the unit ball is the maximum-volume ellipsoid contained in [-1,1]^{n}.
Every ellipsoid contained in K_{\Pi} is contained in the cube, while B_{2}^{n}\subseteq K_{\Pi}.
Hence B_{2}^{n} is the John ellipsoid of K_{\Pi}.
∎
For the stability argument, we also use an enlarged body.
For 0\leq\eta\leq n^{-4}, let
\widehat{K}_{\Pi,\eta}\coloneqq(b+\eta)B_{2}^{n}\cap\bigcap_{u\in\Pi}\{x\colon|\langle u,x\rangle|\leq 1+\eta\}.
(7.2)
The cube is omitted, and hence K_{\Pi}\subseteq\widehat{K}_{\Pi,\eta}.
All fixed-lattice estimates below are uniform for 0\leq\eta\leq n^{-4}.
8 Fixed lattices and separated targets
We first identify a positive-measure set of good torus targets: they have no short residual vector, and both the number of relevant residuals and their aggregate cap cost are O(R).
We then pack this set to obtain exponentially many targets whose residual directions are separated across distinct targets.
Fix a lattice \Lambda, and put
R\coloneqq\frac{\kappa_{n}a^{n}}{\det\Lambda}\quad\text{and}\quad F_{n}\coloneqq n\log n.
(8.1)
We work in the range
c_{*}\leq R\leq c_{0}F_{n},
(8.2)
where c_{*}\coloneqq e^{-\beta}/4 and the upper-range constant c_{0}>0 will be chosen only after the cross-target exponent has been fixed.
The bodies considered below have outer radius b+\eta, with 0\leq\eta\leq n^{-4}.
If such a body covers with lattice \Lambda, then integration of the covering multiplicity gives
\det\Lambda\leq\kappa_{n}(b+\eta)^{n}.
Consequently,
R\geq\left(\frac{a}{b+\eta}\right)^{n}=e^{-\beta+o(1)}\geq\frac{1}{2}e^{-\beta}>c_{*}.
Thus the lower bound in (8.2) excludes no lattice that can cover one of these bodies.
Fix A\coloneqq 10, and let
r_{0}\coloneqq a\exp(-A\log n/n).
For 0\leq\eta\leq n^{-4}, put b_{\eta}\coloneqq b+\eta and define
C_{x}^{\eta}\coloneqq\{u\colon|\langle u,x\rangle|>1+\eta\}\quad\text{and}\quad c_{\eta}(x)\coloneqq\mu(C_{x}^{\eta}).
For y\in\mathbb{T}_{\Lambda}, let
X_{y}^{\eta}\coloneqq(y-\Lambda)\cap\bigl(b_{\eta}B_{2}^{n}\setminus(r_{0}-\eta)B_{2}^{n}\bigr).
Set
m(y)\coloneqq|X_{y}^{\eta}|,\qquad q(t)\coloneqq-\log(1-e^{-t}),\quad\text{and}\quad Q(y)\coloneqq\sum_{x\in X_{y}^{\eta}}q(c_{\eta}(x)).
The quantity 1-e^{-c_{\eta}(x)} is the probability that the cap C_{x}^{\eta} is hit by the Poisson process.
Thus Q(y) is the total logarithmic cost of hitting all residual caps if their dependencies are ignored.
Lemma 8.1.
There are absolute constants C, C_{A}, and \gamma>0 such that, for all sufficiently large n, the following holds uniformly over every lattice satisfying (8.2) and every 0\leq\eta\leq n^{-4}.
The set G_{\Lambda}^{\eta} of targets y that satisfy
(y-\Lambda)\cap(r_{0}-\eta)B_{2}^{n}=\varnothing,\qquad m(y)\leq CR,\quad\text{and}\quad Q(y)\leq CR
(8.3)
has Haar measure at least \gamma.
Moreover, if y is good and x\in X_{y}^{\eta}, then
n^{-C_{A}}\leq c_{\eta}(x)\leq C_{A}.
(8.4)
Proof.
The unfolding identity gives
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{y}m(y)
\displaystyle=\frac{\kappa_{n}(b_{\eta}^{n}-(r_{0}-\eta)^{n})}{\det\Lambda}\leq C_{m}R,
(8.5)
\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{y}\left[(y-\Lambda)\cap(r_{0}-\eta)B_{2}^{n}\neq\varnothing\right]
\displaystyle\leq\frac{\kappa_{n}(r_{0}-\eta)^{n}}{\det\Lambda}\leq 2Rn^{-A}=o(1).
(8.6)
All constants in this proof are uniform in \Lambda and \eta.
Write r=ae^{t/n} in the relevant shell.
Then
c_{\eta}(r)=Mp_{n}\!\left(\frac{r}{1+\eta}\right)\quad\text{and}\quad n\log\frac{r/(1+\eta)}{a}=t-n\log(1+\eta)=t+o(1).
Lemma 6.1(i) therefore gives
C^{-1}e^{t/L}\leq c_{\eta}(r)\leq Ce^{t/L}\quad\text{for}\quad-A\log n-O(1)\leq t\leq\beta+O(1).
(8.7)
This proves (8.4) after enlarging C_{A}=C_{A}(a,A,\beta).
Since a, A, and \beta are fixed, C_{A} is absolute.
For 0<s\leq C_{A}, the function q(s)=-\log(1-e^{-s}) satisfies q(s)\leq C(1+|\log s|).
Applying the unfolding identity again and using the substitution r=ae^{t/n}, we obtain
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{y}Q(y)=\frac{n\kappa_{n}}{\det\Lambda}\int_{r_{0}-\eta}^{b_{\eta}}r^{n-1}q(c_{\eta}(r))\,\mathrm{d}r\leq C_{Q}R\int_{-A\log n-O(1)}^{\beta+O(1)}e^{t}(1+|t|)\,\mathrm{d}t\leq C_{Q}^{\prime}R.
Choose C\geq 8\max\{C_{m},C_{Q}^{\prime}\}.
Markov’s inequality shows that each of the events m(y)>CR and Q(y)>CR has probability at most 1/8.
For sufficiently large n, the probability in (8.6) is at most 1/4.
Hence the three conditions in (8.3) hold on a set of Haar measure at least 1/2.
We may take \gamma\coloneqq 1/2.
∎
If a good target y satisfies m(y)=0, then every residual vector y-\lambda has norm greater than b_{\eta}.
Therefore y is a deterministic hole in \widehat{K}_{\Pi,\eta}+\Lambda.
In the witness construction below, we may consequently restrict attention to good targets with m(y)\geq 1.
We now choose targets whose residual directions are separated across different targets.
Let
\alpha_{\mathrm{sep}}\coloneqq D_{\mathrm{sep}}\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}\quad\text{and}\quad\delta\coloneqq 3\bigl(2\eta+b-r_{0}+b_{\eta}\alpha_{\mathrm{sep}}\bigr),
where D_{\mathrm{sep}} is for now an arbitrary fixed constant.
It will be chosen in Section 9, after the desired cross-target exponent J is fixed.
Suppose that x\in X_{y}^{\eta} and z\in X_{y^{\prime}}^{\eta} have projective angle less than \alpha_{\mathrm{sep}}.
For some sign \varepsilon\in\{-1,1\},
|x-\varepsilon z|\leq 2\eta+b-r_{0}+b_{\eta}\alpha_{\mathrm{sep}}<\delta.
The vector x-\varepsilon z represents y-\varepsilon y^{\prime} on the torus.
The contrapositive of this observation, together with Lemma 6.2, gives the next lemma.
Lemma 8.2.
For every fixed D_{\mathrm{sep}}>0 and all sufficiently large n, there are good targets y_{1},\ldots,y_{T} such that residual directions from distinct targets have projective angle at least \alpha_{\mathrm{sep}}, and
T\geq c\frac{\det\Lambda}{\kappa_{n}\delta^{n}}=\exp\bigl((1/2-o(1))n\log n\bigr).
(8.8)
The estimate is uniform over all lattice shapes satisfying (8.2) and all 0\leq\eta\leq n^{-4}; the o(1) term may depend on the fixed value of D_{\mathrm{sep}}.
Proof.
Apply Lemma 6.2 to G_{\Lambda}^{\eta}.
Since \det\Lambda=\kappa_{n}a^{n}/R and \delta\asymp\sqrt{\log n/n} uniformly in the stated range,
\log\frac{a^{n}}{R\delta^{n}}=\frac{n}{2}\log n-\frac{n}{2}\log\log n+O(n)-O(\log n).
This proves (8.8).
∎
9 Poisson witnesses and the common-lens hierarchy
For a fixed good target, each residual vector in the outer shell determines a cap of Poisson directions that excludes that residual from the random body.
We group nearby residual caps into blocks and place a common measurable slot inside every cap in a block.
An injective Poisson point in each slot then certifies that the target is uncovered.
The hierarchy below controls dependencies among the slots of one target, while the separation from Lemma 8.2 controls dependencies between different targets.
We finally apply the continuous Janson inequality to many targets for which the products of the slot measures are comparable.
We make the constant choices as follows.
The body and shell parameters a, A, and \beta are fixed first.
The geometric estimates in Lemmas 9.2 and 9.3 determine their absolute constants, including A_{0}.
We then fix \varepsilon, take c_{\mathrm{sh}} and B_{0} from Lemma 9.5, and choose a fixed B\geq B_{0}; this determines the anchor exponent C_{\mathrm{anc}}.
These choices are independent of the tail exponent J.
After fixing J>0, we choose D_{\mathrm{sep}}=D_{\mathrm{sep}}(J) sufficiently large for the cross-target estimate and then choose c_{0}=c_{0}(J) sufficiently small.
No constant depends on n, the shape of the lattice, or \eta.
Fix a good target y with m(y)\geq 1, put m\coloneqq m(y), and list its residuals as
X_{y}^{\eta}=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}\}.
For i\in[m], put
C_{i}\coloneqq C_{x_{i}}^{\eta}\quad\text{and}\quad c_{i}\coloneqq\mu(C_{i})=c_{\eta}(x_{i}).
The good-target estimates give
m\leq CR,\qquad m\leq n^{2},\qquad\sum_{i=1}^{m}q(c_{i})\leq CR,\quad\text{and}\quad n^{-C_{A}}\leq c_{i}\leq C_{A}.
(9.1)
The inequality m\leq n^{2} follows from m\leq CR and R\leq c_{0}n\log n for sufficiently large n.
Put
\bar{c}_{i}\coloneqq\min\{c_{i},1/2\}\quad\text{and}\quad s_{i}\coloneqq-\log\bar{c}_{i}.
The truncation keeps the slot scale at most 1/2, while s_{i} records the rarity of the cap.
The metric below combines angular energy with mismatch between these logarithmic intensities.
View e_{i}\coloneqq x_{i}/|x_{i}| as a point of real projective space.
Define
\mathfrak{d}(i,j)\coloneqq\sqrt{n}\,\angle_{\mathrm{proj}}(e_{i},e_{j})+\sqrt{|s_{i}-s_{j}|}.
(9.2)
The projective angle is the geodesic metric on real projective space.
The second summand is also a metric because \sqrt{x+y}\leq\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y} for nonnegative x and y.
Hence \mathfrak{d} is a metric, and
n\angle_{\mathrm{proj}}(e_{i},e_{j})^{2}+|s_{i}-s_{j}|\leq\mathfrak{d}(i,j)^{2}\leq 2n\angle_{\mathrm{proj}}(e_{i},e_{j})^{2}+2|s_{i}-s_{j}|.
(9.3)
For every nonempty set S\subseteq[m], let
r(S)\coloneqq\min_{a\in S}\max_{i\in S}\mathfrak{d}(a,i)^{2}.
(9.4)
The next proposition is the deterministic core of the fixed-target argument.
It partitions the residual caps into blocks and assigns a common-lens slot to each block.
Later, an injective choice of one Poisson point from every slot will certify that the target is a hole.
Estimate (9.5) bounds the negative logarithm of the product of the slot measures, (9.6) controls diagonal identifications, and (9.8) controls off-diagonal identifications after the normalization in (9.7).
The last two estimates feed into the self-diagram bound in Lemma 9.6.
Proposition 9.1.
For all sufficiently large n, every good target y with m(y)\geq 1 has a partition \mathcal{P}_{y} of [m(y)].
For every block S\in\mathcal{P}_{y}, there is a measurable slot
E_{S}\subseteq\bigcap_{i\in S}C_{i},\quad\text{where}\quad 0<\lambda_{S}\coloneqq\mu(E_{S})\leq\frac{1}{2},
such that
\displaystyle\sum_{S\in\mathcal{P}_{y}}-\log\lambda_{S}
\displaystyle\leq CR,
(9.5)
\displaystyle\sum_{S\in\mathcal{P}_{y}}\log(1+\lambda_{S}^{-1})
\displaystyle\leq CR.
(9.6)
For distinct blocks S and T, put
w_{ST}\coloneqq\frac{\mu(E_{S}\cap E_{T})}{\sqrt{\lambda_{S}(1+\lambda_{S})\lambda_{T}(1+\lambda_{T})}}.
(9.7)
Then
\sum_{S\in\mathcal{P}_{y}}\log\left(1+\sum_{T\in\mathcal{P}_{y}\setminus\{S\}}w_{ST}\right)\leq CR.
(9.8)
Every slot has an anchor a(S)\in S such that
E_{S}\subseteq C_{a(S)}\quad\text{and}\quad\lambda_{S}\geq n^{-C_{\mathrm{anc}}}c_{a(S)}.
(9.9)
All constants are uniform in the lattice, the good target, and 0\leq\eta\leq n^{-4}.
9.1 A sharp affinity estimate for caps
The coarse two-cap estimate in Lemma 6.1 has a polynomial prefactor, which is too expensive for the row sum below.
The metric (9.2) also records radial intensity and yields a constant-prefactor estimate.
Lemma 9.2.
For all sufficiently large n and all caps C_{i} and C_{j} belonging to one good target,
\frac{\mu(C_{i}\cap C_{j})}{\sqrt{\bar{c}_{i}\bar{c}_{j}}}\leq C\exp\{-c\mathfrak{d}(i,j)^{2}\}.
(9.10)
The constants are uniform for 0\leq\eta\leq n^{-4}.
Proof.
We first prove an oriented-cap estimate.
Let
H(e,\tau)\coloneqq\{u\colon\langle u,e\rangle>\tau\}\quad\text{and}\quad H(f,\xi)\coloneqq\{u\colon\langle u,f\rangle>\xi\},
where \tau and \xi lie in a fixed compact interval [\tau_{0},\tau_{1}]\subsetneq(0,1).
Put
p(\zeta)\coloneqq\sigma(H(e,\zeta)),\qquad\Delta\coloneqq|\log p(\tau)-\log p(\xi)|,\quad\text{and}\quad t\coloneqq n\psi^{2},
where \psi is the angle between e and f.
One-cap estimates.
Let
c_{n}\coloneqq\frac{\Gamma(n/2)}{\sqrt{\pi}\,\Gamma((n-1)/2)}.
Inserting the factor x into the one-cap integral gives
\frac{c_{n}}{n-1}(1-\zeta^{2})^{(n-1)/2}\leq p(\zeta)\leq\frac{c_{n}}{(n-1)\zeta}(1-\zeta^{2})^{(n-1)/2}.
(9.11)
Since p^{\prime}(\zeta)=-c_{n}(1-\zeta^{2})^{(n-3)/2}, we obtain
\frac{(n-1)\zeta}{1-\zeta^{2}}\leq-\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\zeta}\log p(\zeta)\leq\frac{n-1}{1-\zeta^{2}}.
(9.12)
Consequently,
cn|\tau-\xi|\leq\Delta\leq Cn|\tau-\xi|
(9.13)
uniformly on the threshold interval.
We claim that
\frac{\sigma(H(e,\tau)\cap H(f,\xi))}{\sqrt{p(\tau)p(\xi)}}\leq Ce^{-c(t+\Delta)}.
(9.14)
The intersection is contained in the smaller cap, and hence the left side is at most e^{-\Delta/2}.
Choose a sufficiently large absolute constant K.
If t\leq K(\Delta+1), then this trivial estimate proves (9.14) after adjusting c and C.
We may therefore assume that
t>K(\Delta+1).
(9.15)
By (9.13),
|\tau-\xi|\leq C\frac{\Delta}{n}\leq\frac{C}{K}\psi^{2}.
(9.16)
Two-cap optimization.
Use orthonormal coordinates on \operatorname{span}\{e,f\} in which
e=(1,0)\quad\text{and}\quad f=(\cos\psi,\sin\psi).
The intersection of the two boundary lines is
v_{*}\coloneqq\left(\tau,\frac{\xi-\tau\cos\psi}{\sin\psi}\right).
(9.17)
Writing v_{*}=\omega_{e}e+\omega_{f}f gives
\omega_{e}\coloneqq\frac{\tau-\xi\cos\psi}{\sin^{2}\psi}\quad\text{and}\quad\omega_{f}\coloneqq\frac{\xi-\tau\cos\psi}{\sin^{2}\psi}.
(9.18)
We show that, whenever the cap intersection is nonempty, there is a uniform constant c>0 such that
|v|^{2}\geq|v_{*}|^{2}+c(\delta_{e}+\delta_{f})
(9.19)
for every feasible v, where
\delta_{e}\coloneqq\langle v,e\rangle-\tau\geq 0\quad\text{and}\quad\delta_{f}\coloneqq\langle v,f\rangle-\xi\geq 0,
and that
|v_{*}|^{2}\geq\max\{\tau^{2},\xi^{2}\}+c\min\{\psi^{2},1\}.
(9.20)
Fix a small constant \psi_{0}>0.
If 0<\psi\leq\psi_{0}, then
\omega_{e}=\frac{\tau}{1+\cos\psi}+\frac{(\tau-\xi)\cos\psi}{\sin^{2}\psi}\quad\text{and}\quad\omega_{f}=\frac{\xi}{1+\cos\psi}+\frac{(\xi-\tau)\cos\psi}{\sin^{2}\psi}.
By (9.16), choosing K sufficiently large gives \omega_{e},\omega_{f}\geq c_{\mathrm{lag}}>0.
Since v-v_{*} has inner products \delta_{e} and \delta_{f} with e and f, respectively,
|v|^{2}=|v_{*}|^{2}+2\omega_{e}\delta_{e}+2\omega_{f}\delta_{f}+|v-v_{*}|^{2},
which proves (9.19).
If \tau\geq\xi, then
\xi-\tau\cos\psi=\tau(1-\cos\psi)-(\tau-\xi)\geq c\psi^{2},
and hence
|v_{*}|^{2}-\tau^{2}=\frac{(\xi-\tau\cos\psi)^{2}}{\sin^{2}\psi}\geq c\psi^{2}.
The case \xi\geq\tau is symmetric, so (9.20) follows in the small-angle range.
Suppose now that \psi\geq\psi_{0} and the cap intersection is nonempty.
For a point u in the intersection,
2\tau_{0}\leq\langle u,e+f\rangle\leq|e+f|=2\cos(\psi/2).
Thus \psi\leq\pi-\delta_{0} for some fixed \delta_{0}>0.
When \tau=\xi, the quantities in (9.18) are positive and |v_{*}|^{2}-\tau^{2}=\tau^{2}\tan^{2}(\psi/2) is bounded below on [\psi_{0},\pi-\delta_{0}].
The compactness of this parameter range, together with (9.16), gives uniform positive lower bounds for \omega_{e}, \omega_{f}, and the norm gain when K is sufficiently large.
This proves (9.19) and (9.20) in the remaining range.
Two-dimensional integration.
The first two orthonormal coordinates of a uniform point of \mathbb{S}^{n-1} have density
c_{n,2}(1-|v|^{2})_{+}^{(n-4)/2},\quad\text{where}\quad c_{n,2}\coloneqq\frac{\Gamma(n/2)}{\pi\Gamma((n-2)/2)}=\frac{n-2}{2\pi}.
The map v\mapsto(\delta_{e},\delta_{f}) has Jacobian determinant \sin\psi.
If |v_{*}|\geq 1, then the cap intersection is empty.
Otherwise, let Q\coloneqq 1-|v_{*}|^{2}.
By (9.19),
\displaystyle\sigma(H(e,\tau)\cap H(f,\xi))\leq\frac{c_{n,2}}{\sin\psi}\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\int_{0}^{\infty}(Q-c(\delta_{e}+\delta_{f}))_{+}^{(n-4)/2}\,\,\mathrm{d}\delta_{e}\,\,\mathrm{d}\delta_{f}=\frac{c_{n,2}}{\sin\psi}\frac{4Q^{n/2}}{c^{2}n(n-2)}.
Therefore
\sigma(H(e,\tau)\cap H(f,\xi))\leq\frac{C}{n\sin\psi}(1-|v_{*}|^{2})^{n/2}.
(9.21)
Let \zeta\coloneqq\max\{\tau,\xi\}.
The norm gain (9.20) and compactness of the threshold interval imply
\left(\frac{1-|v_{*}|^{2}}{1-\zeta^{2}}\right)^{n/2}\leq e^{-cn\psi^{2}}.
Dividing (9.21) by the smaller one-cap probability and using (9.11), we obtain
\frac{\sigma(H(e,\tau)\cap H(f,\xi))}{\min\{p(\tau),p(\xi)\}}\leq\frac{C}{\sqrt{n}\sin\psi}e^{-ct}.
In the small-angle range, (9.15) gives \sqrt{n}\sin\psi\asymp\sqrt{t}\geq c\sqrt{K}.
In the large-angle range, \sin\psi is bounded below.
Thus the last expression is at most Ce^{-c^{\prime}t}.
Multiplying by
\sqrt{\frac{\min\{p(\tau),p(\xi)\}}{\max\{p(\tau),p(\xi)\}}}=e^{-\Delta/2}
proves (9.14).
Absolute caps.
Let \tau_{i}\coloneqq(1+\eta)/|x_{i}|.
Then c_{i}=2Mp(\tau_{i}).
Among the four pairs of oriented halves of C_{i} and C_{j}, two have angle \phi=\angle_{\mathrm{proj}}(e_{i},e_{j}), and the other two have angle \pi-\phi\geq\pi/2.
Summing (9.14) over these four pairs gives
\frac{\mu(C_{i}\cap C_{j})}{\sqrt{c_{i}c_{j}}}\leq C\exp\{-c(n\phi^{2}+|\log c_{i}-\log c_{j}|)\}.
(9.22)
Since c_{i}\leq C_{A}, replacing c_{i} by the previously defined \bar{c}_{i} changes the denominator by at most a fixed factor.
Furthermore,
|\log c_{i}-\log c_{j}|\geq|s_{i}-s_{j}|-C.
(9.23)
If neither intensity is truncated, this is equality.
If both are truncated, the right side is zero.
If exactly one is truncated, the two sides differ by at most \log(2C_{A}).
Combining (9.22), (9.23), and (9.3) proves (9.10).
∎
9.2 Scale-sensitive common lenses
Pairwise affinity is not enough to assign an entire cluster of caps to one Poisson point.
The next lemma gives a quantitative common intersection for caps that are close in the parameter metric.
Lemma 9.3.
There is an absolute constant A_{0} with the following property.
Fix B>0, and let n be sufficiently large in terms of B.
If S\subseteq[m], |S|=N\geq 2, and r(S)\leq B\log n, then there exist an anchor a(S)\in S and a measurable set F_{S}\subseteq\bigcap_{i\in S}C_{i} such that
\mu(F_{S})\geq\exp\{-A_{0}(1+r(S)+\log N)\}\bar{c}_{a(S)}.
(9.24)
The anchor may be chosen to minimize c_{i} over i\in S.
Proof.
Choose j_{0}\in S that attains the minimum in (9.4).
Since r(S)\leq B\log n=o(n), every projective direction in S has, for sufficiently large n, a unique representative making angle at most \sqrt{r(S)/n}<\pi/4 with a fixed representative of e_{j_{0}}.
Use these representatives below.
Let i_{0}\coloneqq a(S) minimize c_{i} over S.
By the triangle inequality in projective space, every e_{i} makes angle at most \theta\coloneqq 2\sqrt{r(S)/n} with e_{i_{0}}.
Hence
e_{i}=\cos\phi_{i}\,e_{i_{0}}+\sin\phi_{i}\,w_{i},\quad\text{where}\quad w_{i}\perp e_{i_{0}},\quad|w_{i}|=1,\quad\text{and}\quad 0\leq\phi_{i}\leq\theta.
Let S_{+}\coloneqq\{i\in S\colon\phi_{i}>0\}.
No tangential constraint is needed when \phi_{i}=0.
Put \tau_{i}\coloneqq(1+\eta)/|x_{i}|.
Since c_{i}=2Mp(\tau_{i}) and p is decreasing, the choice of the anchor gives
\tau\coloneqq\max_{i\in S}\tau_{i}=\tau_{i_{0}}.
Choose sufficiently large absolute constants C_{s} and C, in this order, and set
s\coloneqq C_{s}\sqrt{\frac{\log(2N)}{n}}\quad\text{and}\quad h\coloneqq C(\theta s+\theta^{2}).
Because N\leq m\leq n^{2} and r(S)\leq B\log n, we have s=o(1) and h=O_{B}(\log n/n).
Thus \tau+h remains in a fixed compact subinterval of (0,1) for all sufficiently large n.
Condition a uniform vector u\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1} on t=\langle u,e_{i_{0}}\rangle, and write
u=te_{i_{0}}+\sqrt{1-t^{2}}\,w,\quad\text{where}\quad w\in\mathbb{S}^{n-2}.
For every fixed w_{i}, spherical concentration gives
\mathbb{P}_{w}\left[\langle w,w_{i}\rangle<-s\right]\leq e^{-cns^{2}}.
Choose C_{s} so that Ne^{-cns^{2}}\leq 1/2.
A union bound yields
\mathbb{P}_{w}\left[\langle w,w_{i}\rangle\geq-s\text{ for every }i\in S_{+}\right]\geq\frac{1}{2}.
(9.25)
Define
F_{S}\coloneqq\left\{u=te_{i_{0}}+\sqrt{1-t^{2}}\,w\colon t>\tau+h\text{ and }\langle w,w_{i}\rangle\geq-s\text{ for every }i\in S_{+}\right\}.
(9.26)
For u\in F_{S} and i\in S,
\displaystyle\langle u,e_{i}\rangle=t\cos\phi_{i}+\sqrt{1-t^{2}}\sin\phi_{i}\langle w,w_{i}\rangle\geq t\cos\phi_{i}-s\sin\phi_{i}\geq\tau+h-C(\phi_{i}^{2}+s\phi_{i})>\tau_{i}.
The last inequality follows from the choice of C in the definition of h.
Thus F_{S} lies in one oriented half of every C_{i}, and hence F_{S}\subseteq\bigcap_{i\in S}C_{i}.
Integrating first in w and using (9.25), we obtain
\sigma(F_{S})\geq\frac{1}{2}p(\tau+h).
The oriented anchor cap has measure p(\tau), and c_{i_{0}}=2Mp(\tau).
Therefore
\mu(F_{S})\geq\frac{c_{i_{0}}}{4}\frac{p(\tau+h)}{p(\tau)}.
(9.27)
The hazard estimate (9.12) gives
\frac{p(\tau+h)}{p(\tau)}\geq e^{-Cnh}.
Moreover,
nh\leq C\bigl(r(S)+\sqrt{r(S)\log N}\bigr)\leq C^{\prime}\bigl(1+r(S)+\log N\bigr).
Combining the last two estimates with (9.27) and \bar{c}_{i_{0}}\leq c_{i_{0}} proves (9.24).
The resulting constant A_{0} is absolute and does not depend on B.
∎
Increase A_{0} once, if necessary, so that A_{0}\geq 1; this choice is independent of \varepsilon.
Then fix a sufficiently small absolute constant \varepsilon>0.
Define
\ell(S)\coloneqq A_{0}(1+r(S)+\log|S|)\quad\text{when }|S|\geq 2,\quad\text{and}\quad\ell(\{i\})\coloneqq 0.
(9.28)
Let
R_{*}\coloneqq B\log n,
(9.29)
where B is the fixed constant from the hierarchy at the beginning of the section.
A nonempty set S\subseteq[m] is economical if it is a singleton or if
r(S)\leq R_{*}\quad\text{and}\quad\ell(S)\leq\varepsilon|S|.
(9.30)
Start with the partition into singletons.
Whenever at least two current blocks have an economical union, replace those blocks by their union.
Each merge decreases the number of blocks, so the procedure terminates.
Let \mathcal{P}_{y} be a terminal partition.
Every block of \mathcal{P}_{y} is economical, and
no union of at least two blocks of \mathcal{P}_{y} is economical.
(9.31)
For a nonsingleton block S\in\mathcal{P}_{y}, apply Lemma 9.3.
By nonatomicity, choose a measurable subset E_{S}\subseteq F_{S} with
\lambda_{S}\coloneqq\mu(E_{S})=e^{-\ell(S)}\bar{c}_{a(S)}.
(9.32)
For a singleton S=\{i\}, choose E_{S}\subseteq C_{i} with \mu(E_{S})=\bar{c}_{i}, and put a(S)\coloneqq i.
Thus (9.32) holds for every block.
9.3 Terminal local density and weighted rows
Terminality prevents too many low-penalty blocks from having anchors near one point.
The resulting local-count estimate will be converted into the row-sum bound needed for the self-diagram calculation.
Lemma 9.4.
Let T_{\mathrm{loc}},H\geq 0, let N_{0}\geq 1, let z\in[m], and let S_{1},\ldots,S_{N_{0}} be distinct blocks of \mathcal{P}_{y} such that \mathfrak{d}(a(S_{j}),z)^{2}\leq T_{\mathrm{loc}} and \ell(S_{j})\leq H for every j\in[N_{0}].
If
8T_{\mathrm{loc}}+8H/A_{0}\leq R_{*},
(9.33)
then
N_{0}\leq C(1+T_{\mathrm{loc}}+H).
(9.34)
Proof.
Let U\coloneqq S_{1}\cup\cdots\cup S_{N_{0}} and M_{U}\coloneqq|U|.
For each j, choose i_{j}\in S_{j} that attains the minimum in the definition of r(S_{j}).
If i\in S_{j}, then the triangle inequality gives
\mathfrak{d}(i,a(S_{j}))\leq\mathfrak{d}(i,i_{j})+\mathfrak{d}(i_{j},a(S_{j}))\leq 2\sqrt{r(S_{j})}\leq 2\sqrt{H/A_{0}}.
Using a(S_{1}) as a center and applying the triangle inequality through z and a(S_{j}), we obtain
\mathfrak{d}(a(S_{1}),i)\leq 2\sqrt{T_{\mathrm{loc}}}+2\sqrt{H/A_{0}}.
Consequently,
r(U)\leq 8T_{\mathrm{loc}}+8H/A_{0}\leq R_{*}.
The conclusion is immediate when N_{0}=1.
Suppose that N_{0}\geq 2.
Then
\ell(U)\leq A_{0}+8A_{0}T_{\mathrm{loc}}+8H+A_{0}\log M_{U}.
Choose C so large that
A_{0}+8A_{0}T_{\mathrm{loc}}+8H\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{2}M_{U}
whenever M_{U}\geq N_{0}>C(1+T_{\mathrm{loc}}+H), and enlarge C so that A_{0}\log u\leq\varepsilon u/2 for every u\geq C.
If N_{0}>C(1+T_{\mathrm{loc}}+H), then \ell(U)\leq\varepsilon|U|.
Thus U is an economical union of at least two terminal blocks, contrary to (9.31).
This contradiction proves (9.34).
∎
For every block S\in\mathcal{P}_{y}, put
L_{S}\coloneqq-\log\lambda_{S}=s_{a(S)}+\ell(S).
(9.35)
By Lemma 9.2, slot containment, and (9.32),
w_{ST}\leq C\exp\left\{\frac{\ell(S)+\ell(T)}{2}-c\mathfrak{d}(a(S),a(T))^{2}\right\}.
(9.36)
The elementary bound \mu(E_{S}\cap E_{T})\leq\min\{\lambda_{S},\lambda_{T}\} also gives
w_{ST}\leq e^{-|L_{S}-L_{T}|/2}\leq 1.
(9.37)
Lemma 9.5.
There are absolute constants c_{\mathrm{sh}}>0 and B_{0}>0 such that, for every fixed B\geq B_{0} and all sufficiently large n, every S\in\mathcal{P}_{y} with L_{S}\leq c_{\mathrm{sh}}R_{*} satisfies
\sum_{T\in\mathcal{P}_{y}\setminus\{S\}}w_{ST}\leq C(1+L_{S}).
(9.38)
Proof.
Every positive weight w_{ST} lies in a unique interval \bigl(e^{-(k+1)},e^{-k}\bigr].
For k\geq 0, let \mathcal{N}_{k}(S) be the set of blocks T\neq S whose weight lies in this interval.
By (9.37),
|L_{S}-L_{T}|\leq 2(k+1)\quad\text{and}\quad\ell(T)\leq L_{T}\leq L_{S}+2(k+1).
The lower bound w_{ST}>e^{-(k+1)}, together with (9.36), implies
\mathfrak{d}(a(S),a(T))^{2}\leq C_{2}(1+L_{S}+k).
Apply Lemma 9.4 with
z=a(S),\qquad T_{\mathrm{loc}}=C_{2}(1+L_{S}+k),\quad\text{and}\quad H=L_{S}+2(k+1).
There is a sufficiently small absolute constant c_{1}>0 such that the range condition (9.33) holds whenever L_{S}+k+1\leq c_{1}R_{*}.
Hence
|\mathcal{N}_{k}(S)|\leq C_{3}(1+L_{S}+k)
(9.39)
in this range.
Choose c_{\mathrm{sh}}\leq c_{1}/4 and let K\coloneqq\lfloor c_{1}R_{*}/2\rfloor.
Then (9.39) holds for 0\leq k\leq K.
All remaining weights are at most e^{-K}.
Since |\mathcal{P}_{y}|\leq m\leq n^{2}, there is an absolute B_{0}>0 such that every fixed B\geq B_{0} ensures that me^{-K}\leq 1 for all sufficiently large n.
Therefore
\sum_{T\neq S}w_{ST}\leq C\sum_{k\geq 0}e^{-k}(1+L_{S}+k)+1\leq C^{\prime}(1+L_{S}).\qed
Proof of Proposition 9.1.
For u>0,
-\log\min\{u,1/2\}\leq C(1+q(u)).
The anchors of distinct blocks are distinct.
Hence
\sum_{S\in\mathcal{P}_{y}}s_{a(S)}\leq\sum_{i=1}^{m}s_{i}\leq C\left(m+\sum_{i}q(c_{i})\right)\leq CR.
(9.40)
Every terminal block is economical, so
\sum_{S\in\mathcal{P}_{y}}\ell(S)\leq\varepsilon\sum_{S\in\mathcal{P}_{y}}|S|=\varepsilon m.
(9.41)
Equations (9.35), (9.40), and (9.41) prove (9.5).
Also,
\log(1+\lambda_{S}^{-1})\leq L_{S}+\log 2,
and hence (9.6) follows.
To prove (9.8), call a block shallow when L_{S}\leq c_{\mathrm{sh}}R_{*} and deep otherwise.
Lemma 9.5 bounds the logarithmic row cost of a shallow block by C(1+L_{S}).
For a deep block, (9.37) and |\mathcal{P}_{y}|\leq n^{2} give
\log\left(1+\sum_{T\neq S}w_{ST}\right)\leq C\log n\leq C_{B}L_{S}.
Since |\mathcal{P}_{y}|\leq m\leq CR and \sum_{S\in\mathcal{P}_{y}}L_{S}\leq CR, summing over all blocks proves (9.8).
Finally, every block satisfies r(S)\leq R_{*} and |S|\leq n^{2}, so \ell(S)\leq C_{B}\log n.
Since \bar{c}_{a(S)}\geq c_{a(S)}/(2C_{A}), equation (9.32) gives (9.9) after enlarging the absolute exponent C_{\mathrm{anc}}.
∎
9.4 Self and cross diagrams
For a good target y with m(y)\geq 1, let
\nu_{y}\coloneqq\prod_{S\in\mathcal{P}_{y}}\lambda_{S},
and let Z_{y} count the injective tuples with one Poisson point in every final slot.
If Z_{y}>0, then every residual cap belonging to y is hit.
More precisely, goodness excludes residuals of norm less than r_{0}-\eta.
A residual of norm between r_{0}-\eta and b+\eta is cut by the point chosen for the slot containing its cap, while a residual of norm greater than b+\eta lies outside the outer ball of \widehat{K}_{\Pi,\eta}.
Therefore
Z_{y}>0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y\notin\widehat{K}_{\Pi,\eta}+\Lambda.
(9.42)
By (9.5),
e^{-CR}\leq\nu_{y}\leq 1.
(9.43)
Let D_{yy} denote the self-diagram sum from Lemma 6.4.
The calculation below uses (9.6) for diagonal loops and (9.8), after (9.7), for the off-diagonal partial matching.
Lemma 9.6.
For every good target y with m(y)\geq 1,
\frac{D_{yy}}{\nu_{y}^{2}}\leq e^{CR}.
(9.44)
Proof.
For every block S\in\mathcal{P}_{y}, put \delta_{S}\coloneqq 1+\lambda_{S}^{-1}.
For distinct blocks S and T, put
h_{ST}\coloneqq\frac{\mu(E_{S}\cap E_{T})}{\lambda_{S}\lambda_{T}}.
We first fix the off-diagonal identifications between two copies of the witness and then sum over diagonal loops on the compatible, as-yet-unmatched slots.
Consider two copies of \mathcal{P}_{y}.
Fix an off-diagonal partial matching P between them, and let \deg_{P}(S)\in\{0,1,2\} record whether the block S is used on the left, on the right, or on both sides.
Summing all diagonal loops compatible with P gives
\left(\prod_{S}\delta_{S}\right)\left(\prod_{(S,T)\in P}h_{ST}\right)\left(\prod_{S\colon\deg_{P}(S)>0}\delta_{S}^{-1}\right).
Whenever \deg_{P}(S)\in\{1,2\}, we have \delta_{S}^{-1}\leq\delta_{S}^{-\deg_{P}(S)/2}.
The preceding expression is at most
\left(\prod_{S}\delta_{S}\right)\prod_{(S,T)\in P}\frac{h_{ST}}{\sqrt{\delta_{S}\delta_{T}}}=\left(\prod_{S}\delta_{S}\right)\prod_{(S,T)\in P}w_{ST}.
Summing over all off-diagonal partial matchings and adding the empty matching only enlarges the sum.
Hence
\frac{D_{yy}}{\nu_{y}^{2}}\leq\prod_{S\in\mathcal{P}_{y}}(1+\lambda_{S}^{-1})\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}P\text{ an off-diagonal}\\
\text{partial matching}\end{subarray}}\prod_{(S,T)\in P}w_{ST}.
The first product is at most e^{CR} by (9.6).
If we drop injectivity on the right copy, then
\sum_{P}\prod_{(S,T)\in P}w_{ST}\leq\prod_{S\in\mathcal{P}_{y}}\left(1+\sum_{T\neq S}w_{ST}\right)\leq e^{CR}
by (9.8).
Absorbing the two absolute constants in the exponent proves the lemma.
∎
Fix J>0, and now choose the separation constant D_{\mathrm{sep}}=D_{\mathrm{sep}}(J) promised above.
Index the separated targets by \alpha.
For the target y_{\alpha}, write x_{\alpha,i} for its residuals and \mathcal{P}_{\alpha}, E_{\alpha S}, \lambda_{\alpha S}, and a_{\alpha}(S) for its partition, slots, slot measures, and anchors.
In the estimate below, S\in\mathcal{P}_{\alpha} and T\in\mathcal{P}_{\beta}.
The constants A_{0}, B, and the anchor exponent C_{\mathrm{anc}} are already fixed.
If slots belong to distinct targets, then slot containment, (8.4), and Lemma 6.1(iii) give
\displaystyle\frac{\mu(E_{\alpha S}\cap E_{\beta T})}{\lambda_{\alpha S}\lambda_{\beta T}}\leq\frac{\mu(C_{x_{\alpha,a_{\alpha}(S)}}^{\eta}\cap C_{x_{\beta,a_{\beta}(T)}}^{\eta})}{n^{-2C_{\mathrm{anc}}}c_{\eta}(x_{\alpha,a_{\alpha}(S)})c_{\eta}(x_{\beta,a_{\beta}(T)})}\leq n^{-J-5}.
(9.45)
Here D_{\mathrm{sep}} is chosen sufficiently large.
To verify the last inequality, apply Lemma 6.1(iii) with exponent J+2C_{\mathrm{anc}}+C_{A}+5.
Since each target has at most n^{2} slots,
\rho_{\alpha\beta}\leq n^{-J}\quad\text{for}\quad\alpha\neq\beta.
(9.46)
This completes the choice of D_{\mathrm{sep}}.
All constants entering the self-diagram estimate are already fixed; the only remaining choice is the upper-range constant c_{0}, which is made in the proof of Proposition 9.7.
Thus there is no circular dependence.
Proposition 9.7.
For every fixed J>0, there are constants c=c(J)>0 and c_{0}=c_{0}(J)>0 such that, for all sufficiently large n, the following holds.
If c_{*}\leq R\leq c_{0}F_{n}, then, uniformly for 0\leq\eta\leq n^{-4},
\mathbb{P}\left[\widehat{K}_{\Pi,\eta}+\Lambda=\mathbb{R}^{n}\right]\leq e^{-cn^{J}}.
(9.47)
Proof.
Fix J, and choose D_{\mathrm{sep}} as above.
A good target with m(y)=0 is a deterministic hole, so we may assume that every target selected below has at least one residual.
Let y_{1},\ldots,y_{T} be the separated targets from Lemma 8.2.
For a constant C_{T}=C_{T}(J)>0,
\log T\geq\frac{n}{2}\log n-\frac{n}{2}\log\log n-C_{T}n
(9.48)
for all sufficiently large n.
By (9.43), all values -\log\nu_{y} lie in an interval of length at most CR.
Partition this interval into subintervals of length \log 2.
One bin contains at least
T_{\mathrm{bin}}\geq\frac{T}{C(R+1)}
targets whose activities differ by a factor of less than two.
Since R\leq c_{0}n\log n, taking c_{0} sufficiently small and then n sufficiently large gives
\log T_{\mathrm{bin}}\geq\frac{1}{3}n\log n.
(9.49)
Let \nu be the smallest activity in this bin, and select N targets from it.
Their activities satisfy \nu\leq\nu_{\alpha}<2\nu.
Let C_{\mathrm{sd}} be the constant in Lemma 9.6.
Then
\sum_{\alpha}D_{\alpha\alpha}\leq 4N\nu^{2}e^{C_{\mathrm{sd}}R}.
For distinct targets, (6.16) and (9.46), together with e^{x}-1\leq 2x for 0\leq x\leq 1, give
\sum_{\alpha\neq\beta}D_{\alpha\beta}\leq CN^{2}\nu^{2}n^{-J}.
Also, (\sum_{\alpha}\nu_{\alpha})^{2}\geq N^{2}\nu^{2}.
Applying Lemma 6.4, we obtain
\mathbb{P}\left[Z_{\alpha}=0\text{ for every selected }\alpha\right]\leq\exp\left[-c\min\left\{Ne^{-C_{\mathrm{sd}}R},n^{J}\right\}\right].
(9.50)
Choose
N\coloneqq\left\lceil e^{C_{\mathrm{sd}}R}n^{J}\right\rceil.
(9.51)
This choice is available when c_{0} is sufficiently small.
Indeed,
\log N\leq C_{\mathrm{sd}}c_{0}n\log n+J\log n+O(1).
Choose c_{0} so that C_{\mathrm{sd}}c_{0}<1/4.
For sufficiently large n, the right side is less than (1/3)n\log n, and (9.49) gives N\leq T_{\mathrm{bin}}.
Substitution into (9.50) yields the bound e^{-cn^{J}}.
If \widehat{K}_{\Pi,\eta}+\Lambda covers, then no selected target has a witness, by (9.42).
The covering event is therefore contained in the event on the left side of (9.50).
This proves (9.47).
∎
10 Uniformity over all lattices
We now pass from one fixed lattice to all lattices by a finite-net argument.
Any lattice covering K_{\Pi} has covering radius at most b and hence admits a short basis.
The determinant range then gives a quantitative lower bound on the least singular value of a basis matrix, allowing us to round it to a finite matrix grid.
A hole for the enlarged body is stable under the resulting near-identity linear perturbation.
We take J=6 in Proposition 9.7; the resulting probability e^{-cn^{6}} dominates the grid size \exp(O(n^{3}\log n)).
For a lattice \Lambda, let \operatorname{covrad}(\Lambda) denote its Euclidean covering radius.
For 1\leq i\leq n, let \lambda_{i}(\Lambda) denote its ith successive minimum with respect to B_{2}^{n}.
All unqualified matrix norms in this section are Euclidean operator norms; \|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{F}} denotes the Frobenius norm.
Lemma 10.1.
If \operatorname{covrad}(\Lambda)\leq b, then \Lambda has a basis g_{1},\ldots,g_{n} such that
|g_{i}|\leq Cnb\quad\text{for}\quad 1\leq i\leq n.
Proof.
Jarník’s inequality [18] gives \lambda_{n}(\Lambda)\leq 2\operatorname{covrad}(\Lambda); a modern formulation appears in [3, Eq. (12)].
The Mahler basis estimate [12, Eq. (2.5)] gives a basis satisfying
|g_{i}|\leq\max\{1,i/2\}\lambda_{i}(\Lambda).
Since \lambda_{i}(\Lambda)\leq\lambda_{n}(\Lambda), the desired bound follows.
∎
The enlarged body from (7.2) provides the buffer needed to transfer a hole between nearby lattices.
Lemma 10.2.
Let 0\leq\eta\leq n^{-4}.
Let G be an invertible matrix, let \Lambda\coloneqq G\mathbb{Z}^{n}, and let \mathcal{T} be an invertible linear map.
Suppose that y\notin\widehat{K}_{\Pi,\eta}+\Lambda.
If
\|\mathcal{T}-I\|\leq\frac{\eta}{4(b+\eta)},
then \mathcal{T}y\notin K_{\Pi}+\mathcal{T}\Lambda.
Proof.
Fix z\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}, and put x\coloneqq y-Gz.
Since x\notin\widehat{K}_{\Pi,\eta}, either |x|>b+\eta, or some u\in\Pi satisfies |\langle u,x\rangle|>1+\eta.
In the first case,
|\mathcal{T}x|\geq(1-\|\mathcal{T}-I\|)|x|>(1-\|\mathcal{T}-I\|)(b+\eta)\geq b+\frac{3\eta}{4}\geq b.
In the second case, if |x|\leq b+\eta, then
|\langle u,\mathcal{T}x\rangle|\geq|\langle u,x\rangle|-\|(\mathcal{T}-I)x\|>1+\eta-\frac{\eta}{4}=1+\frac{3\eta}{4}\geq 1.
When |x|>b+\eta, the first estimate applies.
Thus \mathcal{T}x\notin K_{\Pi} for every z\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}.
Since \mathcal{T}x=\mathcal{T}y-\mathcal{T}Gz, the point \mathcal{T}y is not covered by K_{\Pi}+\mathcal{T}\Lambda.
∎
Let c_{\mathrm{fix}} be the upper-range constant supplied by Proposition 9.7 for J=6.
Fix c_{\mathrm{net}}>0 so small that 2c_{\mathrm{net}}\leq c_{\mathrm{fix}}, and put
D_{n}\coloneqq\frac{\kappa_{n}a^{n}}{c_{\mathrm{net}}F_{n}}.
(10.1)
Proposition 10.3.
With probability 1-o(1), no lattice \Lambda with \det\Lambda\geq D_{n} covers K_{\Pi}.
Proof.
Suppose that K_{\Pi}+\Lambda covers.
Since K_{\Pi}\subseteq bB_{2}^{n}, the translates of bB_{2}^{n} also cover.
Hence
\operatorname{covrad}(\Lambda)\leq b\quad\text{and}\quad\det\Lambda\leq\kappa_{n}b^{n}.
(10.2)
The determinant bound follows by integrating the covering multiplicity over a fundamental domain.
Now consider a lattice satisfying (10.2) and \det\Lambda\geq D_{n}.
By Lemma 10.1, it has a basis matrix G^{\prime} whose columns have norm at most Cnb.
Consequently,
\|G^{\prime}\|\leq\|G^{\prime}\|_{\mathrm{F}}\leq Cbn^{3/2}.
Let s_{1}(G^{\prime})\geq\cdots\geq s_{n}(G^{\prime})=s_{\min}(G^{\prime}) be the singular values.
Since
|\det G^{\prime}|=\prod_{i=1}^{n}s_{i}(G^{\prime})\leq s_{\min}(G^{\prime})\|G^{\prime}\|^{n-1},
we have
s_{\min}(G^{\prime})\geq\frac{D_{n}}{(Cbn^{3/2})^{n-1}}\eqqcolon\underline{s}_{n}.
(10.3)
Stirling’s formula gives -\log\kappa_{n}=(n/2)\log n+O(n), and hence
-\log\underline{s}_{n}=O(n\log n).
(10.4)
Set \eta\coloneqq n^{-5}, and define the mesh
\xi_{n}\coloneqq\frac{\eta\underline{s}_{n}}{100n(b+\eta)}.
(10.5)
Let \Gamma_{n}\coloneqq\xi_{n}\mathbb{Z}\cap[-2Cnb,2Cnb] and let \mathcal{B}_{n}^{\mathrm{grid}}\coloneqq\Gamma_{n}^{n\times n}.
Retain the invertible matrices G\in\mathcal{B}_{n}^{\mathrm{grid}} satisfying
\frac{D_{n}}{2}\leq|\det G|\leq 2\kappa_{n}b^{n},
(10.6)
and denote this finite set by \mathcal{G}_{n}.
One entry has at most 1+4Cnb/\xi_{n} possible values.
By (10.4) and \eta=n^{-5},
\log\left(1+\frac{4Cnb}{\xi_{n}}\right)=O(n\log n).
Since there are n^{2} entries,
\log|\mathcal{G}_{n}|=O(n^{3}\log n).
(10.7)
Choose, once and for all, a nearest-point rounding map from [-Cnb,Cnb] to \Gamma_{n}.
Apply it entrywise to G^{\prime} and call the rounded matrix G.
The larger interval in the definition of \Gamma_{n} ensures that the rounded entries remain in the grid box.
Also,
\|G-G^{\prime}\|\leq\|G-G^{\prime}\|_{\mathrm{F}}\leq n\xi_{n}.
(10.8)
By Weyl’s inequality and (10.3),
s_{\min}(G)\geq\underline{s}_{n}-n\xi_{n}\geq\frac{1}{2}\underline{s}_{n}
for sufficiently large n.
In particular, G is invertible.
Put
E\coloneqq(G-G^{\prime})(G^{\prime})^{-1}.
Equation (10.8) gives
\|E\|\leq\frac{n\xi_{n}}{\underline{s}_{n}}=\frac{\eta}{100(b+\eta)}<\frac{1}{2}.
(10.9)
Since G=(I+E)G^{\prime}, every singular value of I+E lies in [1-\|E\|,1+\|E\|].
Therefore
\left|\log\frac{|\det G|}{|\det G^{\prime}|}\right|=|\log|\det(I+E)||\leq 2n\|E\|=O(n^{-4}).
(10.10)
The inequalities D_{n}\leq|\det G^{\prime}|\leq\kappa_{n}b^{n} now imply (10.6) for sufficiently large n.
Thus G\in\mathcal{G}_{n}.
The linear map from the grid lattice to the original lattice is
\mathcal{T}\coloneqq G^{\prime}G^{-1}=(I+E)^{-1}.
By (10.9),
\|\mathcal{T}-I\|\leq\frac{\|E\|}{1-\|E\|}\leq 2\|E\|\leq\frac{\eta}{4(b+\eta)}.
(10.11)
For every retained grid lattice G\mathbb{Z}^{n}, its parameter R satisfies
\frac{e^{-\beta}}{2}=\frac{a^{n}}{2b^{n}}\leq R\leq\frac{2\kappa_{n}a^{n}}{D_{n}}=2c_{\mathrm{net}}F_{n}\leq c_{\mathrm{fix}}F_{n}.
In particular, R\geq c_{*}, so Proposition 9.7 applies uniformly with \eta=n^{-5}.
By (10.7) and a union bound,
\mathbb{P}\left[\widehat{K}_{\Pi,\eta}+G\mathbb{Z}^{n}\text{ covers for some }G\in\mathcal{G}_{n}\right]\leq\exp\bigl(O(n^{3}\log n)-cn^{6}\bigr)=o(1).
(10.12)
On the complementary event, every retained grid lattice has a hole for \widehat{K}_{\Pi,\eta}.
Suppose to the contrary that an actual lattice \Lambda\coloneqq G^{\prime}\mathbb{Z}^{n} with \det\Lambda\geq D_{n} covers K_{\Pi}.
The preceding rounding argument supplies a matrix G\in\mathcal{G}_{n}.
Choose y\notin\widehat{K}_{\Pi,\eta}+G\mathbb{Z}^{n}.
By (10.11) and Lemma 10.2,
\mathcal{T}y\notin K_{\Pi}+\mathcal{T}G\mathbb{Z}^{n}=K_{\Pi}+G^{\prime}\mathbb{Z}^{n},
contrary to the assumed covering.
This contradiction proves the proposition.
∎
11 Proofs of the main results
Proof of Theorem 1.3.
Let V be the event \operatorname{vol}_{n}(K_{\Pi})\geq c_{v}\kappa_{n}a^{n}.
By Proposition 7.1, \mathbb{P}\left[V\right]\geq c_{p}>0.
Let U be the event that no lattice of determinant at least D_{n} covers K_{\Pi}.
By Proposition 10.3, \mathbb{P}\left[U\right]=1-o(1).
Therefore
\mathbb{P}\left[U\cap V\right]\geq\mathbb{P}\left[V\right]-\mathbb{P}\left[U^{\mathrm{c}}\right]\geq c_{p}-o(1)>0
for sufficiently large n.
Fix a realization in U\cap V, and denote the resulting body by K_{n}.
Every lattice \Lambda that covers K_{n} satisfies \det\Lambda<D_{n}.
Hence
\frac{\operatorname{vol}_{n}(K_{n})}{\det\Lambda}\geq\frac{c_{v}\kappa_{n}a^{n}}{D_{n}}=c_{v}c_{\mathrm{net}}n\log n.
Since K_{n} is origin-symmetric by construction, taking the infimum over all covering lattices proves Theorem 1.3 with c=c_{v}c_{\mathrm{net}}.
By Proposition 7.1, the John ellipsoid of K_{n} is B_{2}^{n}.
∎
Proof of Theorem 1.1.
The lower inequality follows from Theorem 1.3.
Every origin-symmetric convex body is a convex body, so the definitions give \Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{sym}}(n)\leq\Theta_{L}^{\mathrm{conv}}(n).
The upper inequality follows from Theorem 1.2.
Taking c from Theorem 1.3 and C and \varepsilon_{n} from Theorem 1.2 proves Theorem 1.1.
∎
